In this study, we identified a prominent issue with the performance of decision-feedback equalizers (DFEs) in underwater fiber transmissions. We observed that severe chromatic dispersion and fiber nonlinearity in these transmissions lead to extended guard periods, resulting in increased symbol error rates (SERs) due to prolonged burst errors. We based our research on a 10Gbase-BR2 fiber-optic transmission link with a 2.7ps/nm smear length and 17.2W/km nonlinear threshold, and used a split-step method to simulate the distorted signal. We found that the DFE's performance degradation could be attributed to the delayed and distorted version of the forward backward recursive algorithm's (FBRA's) feedback symbols. We proposed a modified DFE structure that mitigated this issue by delaying the input data, resulting in a 2-3dB improvement in DFE's bit error rate (BER). However, this solution is not practical due to the increased storage requirement. To address this challenge, we devised a simple and effective method that involves checking the DFE's output for errors before storing the distorted symbol, reducing the error propagation by half. This technique's effectiveness was verified through extensive simulations over various channel conditions, and it demonstrated a notable 5-10dB gain in DFE's BER when compared to the conventional DFE. This optimized DFE scheme was successfully demonstrated in a field trial over a 48.96km underwater fiber link with up to 17.4W/km nonlinear interference, and it delivered a minimum 10^-3 BER with only 0.5dB power margin. Deep Learning based models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have gained popularity in time-series analysis tasks. TCNs use a form of fancy convolution called TFC that is well-suited for modeling dynamics over flexible time periods. However, both convolutional networks and TCNs have difficulty handling data with varying time stamps when the time stamps are the same for different data points, a problem known as the "dilemma of identical stamps." To resolve this issue for data with equally spaced time stamps, a new technique called Trimming In Time (PIT) reduces each data segment to a shorter duration while maintaining the network's original capacity, effectively breaking down equally spaced time stamps into pairs of identical stamps. We demonstrate that applying PIT before training can significantly reduce the number of data samples needed, resulting in substantial gains in training speed and model size for both classification and regression tasks. We also introduce an innovative method to determine the optimal duration for data segmentation, one that considers both the network's capacity and the characteristics of the time-series data. By integrating PIT with other optimization techniques such as quantization and sparse connection reduction, we achieve even greater improvements in model size without compromising accuracy. Our experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on six benchmark datasets across four task types, and the source code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-NGNet/tree/main/triming_in_time. Moreover, we identify a particular subalgebra within the free 3-generator Zinbiel algebra that possesses a simple subalgebra and meets the requirements for a finite-dimensional simple Zinbiel algebra in the case where the base field is the real numbers. This real subalgebra then serves as the basis for an infinite series of simple Zinbiel algebras over the real numbers. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
limited and accurately annotated object-to-pose mappings. By extending object
points with relative poses, NDFs offers a complete description of an object's
configuration. We develop a format for pose descriptors that remains invariant
regarding rotation and translation. By encoding this information in a point cloud
relative to the object's reference frame, we ensure the descriptor's integrity.
Using minimal descriptor data, we train a format-agnostic model predicting both
object points and relative poses. Our experiments demonstrate NDF's ability to
generalize across different poses and objects not seen during training. It out
performs existing models when applied to tasks like object reconstruction, pose
classification, and grasping. NDF shows particular strength in tasks involving
limited and noisy data, making it suitable for scenarios with restricted access
to labeled data. Our findings suggest that rotational and translational poses can
be differentiated based on subtle features in 3D descriptor point clouds. The
code is available at https://github.com/google-neural-osrf/neural-descriptor-fields.

To compensate for larger emission spectra and increased photon production, the SiD's sensor layer is being reviewed for enhancement. Initially, the SiD was designed with five thin sensor layers for minimum material, but now it seems that increasing the photon collection with more sensitive devices could be more effective than reducing material. This approach may allow for the reduction of sensor layers to three while maintaining efficient particle detection. Upgrading the sensors to sensitive devices with less readout noise may also facilitate the use of smaller beams and reduced material within the detector, leading to increased detection precision and better track finding. This revision keeps the 3-layer SiD design on track to achieve the desired performance at the ILC, even under conditions expected for luminosities exceeding 250 fb^-1 at 1 TeV center-of-mass energy. This revised design also considers the implications of larger emission spectra on the vertex layer and the need for improved vertex finding, but this in turn may be addressed by increasing the vertex resolution rather than changing the vertex layer design. The revised 3-layer SiD detector meets the detector performance requirements outlined by the ILC Steering Committee and sets a suitable performance standard for the final detector design before construction begins. To address this limitation, we propose a new method for generating molecules using a simpler set of rules that are easier to train for machine learning models. This technique involves defining two sets of rules: one for molecules with known activities that serve as targets, and another for all potentially feasible molecules. Our strategy derives the parameters for these rules using linear regression and formulates the problem of finding optimal molecule parameters as an integer optimization problem. By applying this technique to the design of polymers, we show that our approach outperforms the original framework and matches the performance of a leading commercial tool. Additionally, our results demonstrate that our method achieves comparable or better accuracy with less complex models, and we provide insights into designing efficient models for polymer derivation. To facilitate further research, we are releasing our code under an open-source framework called PolyDerive, which is available on GitHub. With PolyDerive, we are confident that our approach will inspire innovations in the development of more complex molecules. To that end, we are excited to announce that PolyDerive has been selected as one of the winning solutions in the 2022 AMFF Data Science Challenge. The foundation theorem in the theory of automata and formal languages originates from Chomsky's work on context-free languages. It states that every context-free language contains a subset that corresponds to context-free grammars in a more simplified form. This context-free subset can be generated by deterministic context-free languages, which in turn can be recognized by deterministic pushdown automata. The foundation theorem implies that the language families defined by deterministic pushdown automata and context-free languages are equivalent. This notion of the foundation theorem has been expanded upon in the theory of abstract automata and monoids. Here, we present an extension of the foundation theorem to the B-type Coxeter groups, providing a theoretical basis for the connection between deterministic pushdown automata and context-free languages within this more general framework. This involvement of the B-type Coxeter groups renders the foundation theorem independent of the ordering of generators and words, as well as allowing for a more nuanced view of the intersection and union operations in context-free languages. The proof of the foundation theorem for the B-type Coxeter groups relies on the properties of the order relation and word order in these groups, and demonstrates that these groups serve as a universal framework for determining the context-free nature of languages. Furthermore, this theory can be applied to resolve some long-standing open problems and conjectures in the field of context-free languages. The name "foundation theorem" may be seen as a tribute to the significant influence that Chomsky's work has had on the development of the theory of abstract automata and monoids. Additionally, we provide a historical account of the foundation theorem and its extensions within the context of formal languages and abstract automata, highlighting the key contributions of various researchers over the years. A novel type of integrated photonic component known as a T-shaped hub has been designed for use in next-generation nanophotonic systems.  This device architecture offers exceptional light confinement properties and high nonlinearity requirements, making it an ideal platform for detecting small changes in a surrounding medium.  To understand the effect of a T hub on light propagation, we performed a theoretical analysis and observed that this device can serve as a sensitive medium for detecting changes in the refractive index near the taper tip.  To utilize the low-electron mobility of silicon to enhance optical detection capabilities, we propose incorporating a source of light within the hub design.  Through simulation, we showed that a T hub can achieve high detection rates of up to 10 Gb/s in a 10 ps time frame and have designed an applicable unit based on these simulations.  Further development of this design into a working device is pending the advancement of low-loss silicon photonic technologies.  Until then, studying the effect of a T hub on light propagation will provide valuable insights into the future development of nanophotonic systems. MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging techniques, such as contrast agents, improve diagnostic accuracy by highlighting specific internal functions and malfunctions. Visual inspection of MRI images involves experienced eyes to detect abnormal patterns, but this method's effectiveness relies on the radiologist's expertise and can be inconsistent. To address this limitation, automated tumor detection methods have been developed, combining image processing techniques to create efficient algorithms. These algorithms analyze MRI images to identify specific characteristics and locations, reducing reliance on visual inspection and enhancing the consistency of tumor detection. Given the success of automated detection methods in other imaging technologies, such as mammography, it is essential to explore their application in MRI tumor analysis. This research review introduces various image processing techniques, including thresholding, gradient-based methods, edge detection, regional growth algorithms, and neural networks, which can be adapted for MRI tumor detection. However, each method has its own strengths and weaknesses, making it essential to carefully evaluate and compare their performance on MRI data. A survey of the literature reveals that the most effective algorithms for MRI tumor detection rely on robust feature extraction methods and rigorous experimentation to fine-tune their parameters, thus minimizing the risk of premature convergence and optimal solution attainment. Consequently, further research is needed to establish standardized performance evaluation criteria for automated MRI tumor detection, enabling clear guidance on the selection of suitable image analysis methods and efficient solution optimization techniques. This, in turn, will facilitate more comparative studies and a deeper understanding of the interrelations between performance metrics, problem representation, solution optimization, and the underlying biology of tumors. Ultimately, a comprehensive exploration of image analysis methods and optimization techniques will ultimately contribute to the development of reliable, efficient, and robust automated systems for the detection of tumors in MRI images. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity can mask the signals from these celestial bodies. To improve the sensitivity of planet detection, it is essential to develop effective techniques for suppressing the effects of stellar activity. One such method, least-squares deconvolution (LSD), can achieve this by reducing the noise associated with stellar activity when analyzing spectral lines. However, the performance of this method relies on the selection of lines, which can vary depending on the source. To assess the effectiveness of line selection in minimizing the effects of stellar activity and enhancing planet detection, we examined two different line catalogs: a parametric line list based on molecular data and a randomized line set. The results showed that the performance of LSD line selection is highly dependent on the characteristics of the lines chosen, with the molecular-based selection resulting in better deconvolution outcomes. Furthermore, a randomized line set failed to deliver comparable performance even with an optimal normalization, despite our best efforts to optimize the line selection. Therefore, we recommend utilizing line lists based on molecular data, particularly those derived from the Vienna Atomic Line Database, for the purpose of LSD. To this end, we present a new line list comprising 31,629 lines, which can be downloaded from the electronic archive provided. Additionally, we explored the potential benefits of using randomized line sets, keeping open the possibility of exploring alternative line selection strategies in future research. To this end, we have made the randomized line sets we examined available for download as well. To evaluate the effectiveness of LSD in detecting exoplanets, we employed a parametric approach that incorporated information on the planetary system in question, incorporating constraints on the orbital periods, masses, and eccentricities of potential celestial bodies. This methodology was applied to data sets covering the H-alpha and CaII line ranges, with the goal of identifying the most suitable line catalogs for LSD. Our analysis indicated that the performance of LSD differed significantly depending on the line list employed, with some line sets delivering better deconvolution outcomes than others. Ultimately, our research identified an optimal line list for LSD, which minimizes the effects of stellar activity while detecting exoplanes, providing a valuable framework for enhancing the sensitivity of planet detection. This is particularly relevant for the detection of long-period exoplanets, which are frequently host stars with high levels of activity. In our research, we re-examine how object context influences the object recognition capabilities of deep neural networks, with a focus on identifying the most informative context features. Through extensive experiments, we find that when objects are positioned far apart within an image, their placement does not affect recognition performance. In contrast, the presence of nearby objects whose orientations are varied, has a significant impact on the network's ability to accurately identify the central object. We propose a straightforward method to determine the most informative visual features related to object context, which is subsequently utilized to create a context similarity metric. This metric is then used to investigate the underlying factors influencing object context, including the network's inherent biases and the data used for training, among others. Furthermore, we find that improving the network's performance on challenging images also enhances its performance in corresponding context scenarios. We share a comprehensive set of results, along with reproducibility guidelines, for the sake of advancing the field. We argue that our findings are relevant to all deep object recognizers, which are primarily based on convolutional neural networks. Additionally, we provide context similarity scores for a broad range of scenes, as well as context-aware models that can be employed in conjunction with existing deep recognizers. These integrated systems can be used in various context-related applications. We also introduce a novel evaluation approach called context-aware closed-loop evaluation, which involves assessing the performance of these systems on a dataset that mimics real-world scenarios. Through this evaluation process, we identify certain situations where state-of-the-art networks underperform when compared to human subjects. Further analysis of these instances reveals that they often involve unusual layouts or incorporate semantic similarities that can affect the interpretation of context. We discuss potential strategies to overcome these challenges, which could involve incorporating additional visual information or using a more comprehensive definition of context. We conclude that, despite the significant progress made by deep object recognizers, they still struggle with complex context-related tasks. Therefore, it is essential to acknowledge these limitations and strive for the development of more robust systems that can effectively utilize context to improve their performance. We believe that achieving this goal requires a deeper understanding of how context affects the interpretation of images and triggers unintended effects due to the network's architecture and training data. This study explains the double spin difference observed in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, specifically focusing on the cosine of the azimuthal angle collective phenomenon. Our calculation demonstrates that this phenomenon arises from the interference between the transverse momentum dependent (SOTF) correlators and the hadron spin density, which is compelled by scale invariance. In addition, our analysis reveals that the cosine of the azimuthal angle collective phenomenon is intrinsic to the hadron level and governs the sidis cross section at the hadron level, resulting in the observed deviation in data without requiring additional assumptions. Our analysis also identifies the cosine of the azimuthal angle collective phenomenon in sidis as a critical factor in determining hadron spin density and, in turn, the spin structure function $g_1$, particularly at large $x$. Furthermore, this study highlights that the cosine of the azimuthal angle collective phenomenon leads to a hadron mass effect, quantifying the contribution to the spin density and $g_1$ up to $x \approx 0.4$. Our analysis predicts that the observed deviation in sidis will increase with higher $x$, exceeding the quark model expectation by a factor of five to six. This study also suggests that the double spin sidis on the deuteron, $d\sigma^{d\uparrow i\uparrow}$, will exhibit a hadron mass dependence comparable to $d\sigma^{p\uparrow p\uparrow}$. Our analysis provides clear experimental signatures to identify the cosine of the azimuthal angle collective phenomenon and hadron spin density, thereby laying out a pathway for deciphering the spin structure of hadrons. This study is a follow-up to our previous work on the same topic in scattering processes off an unpolarized target. Additionally, we provide an explanation for a recently observed deviation in double longitudinally polarized sidis and an associated prediction for the double spin difference in sidis on the proton and deuteron, encompassing explanations for collective phenomena in single sidis and the famous spin crisis in deep inelastic scattering. Our analysis reveals that the spin density, compelled by scale invariance, is the root cause of the double spin difference in sidis, resulting in a hadron spin density that is intricate and multifaceted, reflecting the collective nature of hadrons governed by QCD. This study is a comprehensive exploration of the role of scale invariance in sidis and scattering processes off an unpolarized and polarized target, providing a clear understanding of hadron spin properties

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity suggestion framework with a layered graph representation. The proposed approach utilizes Wikipedia pages as a knowledge base and constructs a layered graph to facilitate entity suggestions. We extract features from Wikipedia categories to characterize both users and entities, thereby creating a user entity profile. This profile serves as a starting point for entity suggestions, with users able to select entities that align with their preferences. To further refine suggestions, we develop a method to acquire additional entity features from Wikipedia's hidden structure, which is derived from latent category assignments to entity pages. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of our approach through a Wikipedia-based entity suggestion evaluation, finding it to be a more robust and user-friendly alternative to traditional list-based entity suggestion methods. Furthermore, we observe improvements in user experience and entity suggestion quality. Additionally, we discuss the scope for expanding our approach to accommodate more complex entities and provide insights into designing an intuitive user interface for entity suggestions. Our approach and experiments are made open source available for replication. Moreover, we introduce an innovative strategy to tackle entity drift, addressing changes in user preferences over time, which is to be explored in depth in future work. The proposed approach holds promise for applications such as virtual assistants and content creation platforms that rely heavily on entity suggestions. The Ideal Kidney Exchange Program involves pairings of kidney donors and recipients based on compatibility, where two pairs that cannot exchange kidneys directly can do so in a tripleting situation involving a third compatible pair. This program's purpose is to increase the likelihood of kidney transplants for those with hard-to-match antibodies by utilizing a larger network of potential donors. We are examining a static model that represents the Ideal Kidney Exchange Program, where the goal is to maximize the number of transplants within a given set of pairs capable of exchanging kidneys. Our focus is on understanding whether this ideal maximum number of transplants can be achieved through a local search method from initially random pairings. This involves investigating whether such a search algorithm can locate and move through all ideal solutions, which would imply having a mechanism to determine whether a given set of pairings is optimal. We prove that in situations with only two pairs, we can find ideal solutions, and with three pairs, the likelihood of finding one is at least 75%. Furthermore, we find that this likelihood increases with the number of pairs capable of exchanging kidneys. Additionally, we observe that in cases where we are highly unlikely to find an ideal solution, it is because a particular type of pair dominates the search process. We propose a method to reduce the likelihood of this phenomenon occurring and provide evidence that this modification results in a search path that visits all ideal solutions more efficiently. We also provide theoretical support, confirming that our results align with the ideal solution distribution as predicted by a model from one of the paper's co-authors. Finally, we include results from conducting multiple searches through all ideal solutions and provide statistical evidence to support our findings. We believe that these results will be useful in assessing the effectiveness of the Ideal Kidney Exchange Program. We plan to explore possible connections with other graph optimization problems and discuss how the program's challenges could be addressed using different search methods. Lastly, we propose a new problem, ideal cycles, that is related to ideal pairings and could serve as an alternative way to verify whether a given set of pairings is optimal. We have demonstrated that this new problem shares a connection with a well-known graph theory problem and have provided evidence that searching for ideal solutions through cycle representations is a more efficient method than searching through all possible pairings. This assumption is thoroughly examined for each wordlist category through comprehensive experiments consisting of linear classifications and the introduction of novel evaluation metrics that assess the comprehensibility of word representations with respect to the dictionary's nuances. Our results indicate that certain word representations achieve impressive classification accuracies but fail to comprehend the dictionary's nuances as intended. To further improve the method, we enhance the embedded boundary technique by utilizing a blended function that smooths the transition at the boundary, reducing the typical singularity there. We apply this hybrid method to a melting-kernels problem and compare it with standard level-set and embedded boundary approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential advantages. To resolve issues with advection in the level-set approach, we explore the utilization of staggered finite volume and control volume finite element methods as alternative methods for solving the advection-diffusion equation. In the context of searching for optimal solutions in search and retrieval scenarios involving multiple players, we investigate how the Best Map Worst Protocol (BMPW) approach behaves. The BMPW strategy involves each player selecting their best possible equilibrium based on their individual preferences and the actions of the other players. We demonstrate that if all players employ this approach, it leads to a situation where the most rationalizable equilibria are identified, provided that the number of possible strategies for each player is limited. However, this outcome may be distorted if some players are able to select the most optimal equilibria. Furthermore, we find that if search costs are incorporated, the BMPW approach results in the most rationalizable equilibria being reached, but only under the assumption that search costs do not influence players' choices of equilibrium. We also examine how a variety of search protocols, including ones that incorporate learning mechanisms, perform in comparison to the BMPW approach. Additionally, we investigate how player preferences, the number of players, and the characteristics of the search space influence the effectiveness of the BMPW approach. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$. Additionally, we find that on Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a contraction or expansion Cotton soliton cannot exist, while a steady Cotton soliton may exist on these manifolds. We also conclude that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds where the Reeb vector field is an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a contraction or expansion Cotton soliton cannot exist, with a steady Cotton soliton possibly existing on these manifolds. Moreover, we find that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds where the Reeb vector field forms a gradient vector field, a contraction or expansion Cotton soliton cannot exist, with a steady Cotton soliton possibly existing on these manifolds. To address this issue, a prominent technique called reinforcement learning with reward summerization is proposed, which compresses the data collected during training, enabling the discovery of more effective strategies. When tested on three distinct games, the proposed technique demonstrates superior performance when compared to conventional experience replay methods. Furthermore, results indicate that variance decrease based experience replay yields more resilient policies, outperforming other compared methods by a significant margin. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific class of techniques, known as the Eliminate-Win design, addresses this challenge by first identifying and resolving conflicts, followed by the consistent propagation of updates. This framework is the foundation for conflict-free replicated data structures. We introduce a conflict resolution approach for last-writer-wins types of operations over replicated arrays, which serves as the basis for further development of Eliminate-Win designs. Our approach is efficient, running in O(kn) time, where n represents the number of replicas and k the size of the updated array, and is capable of handling a high volume of operations. To better understand the interactions between genomic variations and traits, researchers have developed two methods for studying the genome: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and functional genomic analysis. GWAS examine large populations for specific trait associations with particular genetic locations, while functional genomic data looks at the active genetic functions across the entire genome. Both approaches have limitations, with GWAS often focusing on individual traits and ignoring the complexity of the genome, while functional genomic data may not directly address the link between genetic functions and traits. To overcome these restrictions, researchers have developed new tools to combine GWAS and functional genomic data, based on the idea that the active genetic functions in a particular region are more likely to contribute to the development of a certain trait. By applying these combined approaches to 18 different traits, researchers have found that the associated genetic regions tend to be more actively involved in various biological processes and often display distinct patterns of activity across different cell types. For example, the genetic regions associated with type 2 diabetes are more actively involved in cellular processes related to cell growth and metabolism, particularly in cells from the pancreas and other tissues that are directly affected by the disease. In contrast, the genetic regions linked to an increased risk of developing skin cancer are more actively involved in processes related to cell growth and the repair of damaged DNA, but show no difference in activity compared to areas of the genome not associated with the disease. By considering both the functional aspects of the genome and the link to specific traits, researchers have gained a more comprehensive understanding of how different parts of the genome contribute to the development of complex traits. Furthermore, by looking at the active genetic functions across the entire genome, researchers have identified patterns of cellular processes that are associated with an increased risk of developing certain diseases, even if the specific genetic locations cannot be identified. This understanding enables us to derive all weights of modular forms, including those that are not geometric, as combinations of geometric weights subject to an extended version of the congruence theorem. This insight allows us to demonstrate the diversity of the non-geometric weights of modular forms for S3 through an explicit calculation, suggesting that they form a larger group than the geometric weights do. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has demonstrated that incremental learning algorithms can tackle the stream challenge, although they typically assume a balanced dataset. Conversely, real-world datasets frequently exhibit an uneven distribution of classes, further complicating the learning process. The problem is exacerbated by the fact that deep models often struggle to adapt to new classes and prioritize learning from easily identifiable minority classes over minority, unseen classes. As a result, they develop a poor understanding of the minority classes and the majority classes are often confused with the background. Present strategies for tackling dataset imbalance are mainly centered around oversampling the minority class, reducing the majority class, or giving more importance to the minority class during the learning process. Meanwhile, novel techniques for dealing with the issue of data imbalance in deep learning have emerged, although a comprehensive evaluation of these methods in the context of inc
remental learning is still pending. This work delves into a comprehensive evaluation of different techniques for dealing with data imbalance, including both legacy methods and cutting-edge approaches, in the setting of incremental learning. The evaluation is conducted across multiple benchmark datasets and a distinct evaluation protocol is adopted to ensure the validity of the findings. The results indicate that both legacy and cutting-edge approaches yield superior performance when compared to a baseline scenario, despite the complexities inherent to incremental learning. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. Through extensive evaluation across multiple datasets, our results demonstrate substantial gains in accuracy and convergence speed when compared to baseline methods, including those employing face verification features. A key advantage of decentralized energy systems lies in their resilience to the disruptions caused by the growing presence of photovoltaic systems and self-sufficiency in electricity distribution. Nevertheless, the changing behavior of electricity demand due to the presence of storage devices may counterbalance this benefit. Consequently, it is crucial to examine how self-sufficiency patterns are affected by the adoption of storage technology. Existing studies on self-sufficiency usually rely on representative household types, but this approach fails to account for how storage influences individual behavior and flexibility. Therefore, we introduce an agent-based model that simulates household decision-making and explores how storage impacts self-sufficiency and flexibility. Our analysis indicates that storage induces a self-sufficiency effect, leads to increased flexibility during peak sunshine hours, and results in a counterintuitive flexibility reduction in the middle of the day. Furthermore, we show that the flexibility provided by storage is valuable enough to cover the costs of acquisition, but also highlight the risk of over-planning, especially when the ability to trade flexibility among agents is introduced. Our research provides valuable insights for policymakers seeking to balance the benefits of decentralized energy systems with those of individual storage adoption. Finally, we conclude that there is scope for innovative pricing mechanisms that take full advantage of the changing behavior caused by storage and PV systems, and that these changes may very well increase self-sufficiency and flexibility even further. Our model is based on real data from Swiss households, but the issues it raises are relevant to any country where self-sufficiency and storage adoption are becoming more common. Therefore, there is a significant need for further research into how storage influences individual behavior and flexibility within the broader context of decentralized energy systems. Nevertheless, the value of its ability to provide flexibility that is valuable enough to cover the costs of acquiring it is a finding that is likely to apply widely. Now, through the use of an x-ray pulse generated by an x-ray free-electron laser and an atomic state created by an ultrashort, intense x-ray pulse, we are able to observe the correlation between electrons in rare gases over a sub-femtosecond to sub-cycle time scale.  A theoretical model demonstrates that, in certain conditions, the distribution of electron pairs can be influenced by an electric field with an intensity of $10^{11}$ Watts per square meter and that this effect can serve as an atomic scale generator of polarization in an x-ray pulse. Our investigation into the conductive properties of a two-dimensional HgTe layer, where electrons behave like massless Dirac particles, shows that quantum conduction dominates when a strong magnetic field is applied through a parallel direction to the layer. This phenomenon is driven by the absence of a energy gap in HgTe and is not limited to a specific range of magnetic field strengths. Our research indicates that the critical point where the conduction transitions from quantum to classical occurs at an incredibly high electric field of approximately 10$^7$ V/m. Notably, this transition can be modulated through changes in the intensity of an applied light, which in turn influences the carrier concentration without closing the energy gap. This leads to a fascinating separation of the effects on the system, where the quantum conduction is shown to be independently controlled by the carrier concentration and a strong magnetic field. This result has significant implications for the design of magnetic field-controlled quantum conduction in HgTe layers. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink transmissions flexibly, depending on current traffic conditions, but this self-adaptive approach can cause conflicts between neighboring cells, limiting the effectiveness of DTDD. We have developed a new method that applies noncooperative game theory to resolve these conflicts and maximize each cell's overall throughput. Our solution, based on a subgame perfect equilibrium strategy, ensures maximum possible throughput for every cell and is achievable through a hybrid of centralized and decentralized decision-making. To illustrate the efficacy of this method, we conducted simulations under various traffic scenarios and found that our approach yields results only 5% shorter of optimal in an ideal scenario, but significantly better in scenarios with more variability. By reducing the frequency of schedule changes from once every 10 seconds to once every 60 seconds, we saw an expected increase of 1.5% in overall throughput. We also observed that our method can adapt quickly to changes in traffic conditions. For a medium-sized network with 100 cells, we found that cells with the lowest initial traffic loads tend to see the greatest increases in throughput, but also the greatest variability. We are currently exploring ways to minimize schedule changes and reduce the impact of power control on DTDD performance. Our investigation focuses on a specific square, namely the one based on the E$_8$ lattice, and we aim to describe its underlying dimensions. Namely, we are looking to identify the finite-dimensional space that contains the primary algebra's Peierls weight, which is closely related to its depth. To approach this problem, we draw inspiration from Ito's work, utilizing his strategy to handle the Haagerup's question about the Asymptotic Operator Algebra of type $C_2$ unitary fusion categories. HNNs are distinctive in utilizing Hamiltonian Dynamics to predict changes in data probabilities, thereby producing precise gradient data without the need for backward propagation. This unique characteristic raises intriguing questions about the underlying connection between HNNs and the concept of gradient estimation via optimization. This limitation results in biased outputs from HNNs in comparison to their deterministic network counterparts. To mitigate this bias, we introduce a novel objective function that encourages the generation of synthetic noise in order to render gradients from HNNs comparable to those from standard neural networks. As graph-based data is increasingly utilized in various applications, protecting the connectivity information of graphs has become a pressing concern. Research into differential privacy aims to safeguard sensitive data by controlling the discrepancy of information disclosure. This topic is highly relevant to graph-based data, which is subject to leakage through node rankings and shortest paths. This survey paper provides an in-depth examination of existing work on differential secrecy within the context of graph structures, emphasizing various attacks that expose private information and countermeasures developed to defend against these attacks. We offer a comprehensive framework that organizes current contributions and future research directions in this field. This survey consists of three primary sections: (1) attacks on graph-based data, which includes rankings and paths, and (2) countermeasures that incorporate different private tools, and (3) future research directions and open problems. These issues are particularly challenging in dynamic graphs and require innovative solutions. All together, this survey provides a thorough overview of the topic, its current state, and its potential evolution. Words: 249. The standard theoretical framework used to study binary neutron star mergers involves a neutron star in an accretion disk breaking apart, with interacting multi-dimensional physics including a disk, a hyper-accreting black hole, and a deformed neutron star. For the merger's electromagnetic behavior, researchers typically focus on the interaction between the neutron star and the disk, while modeling the neutron star using 1.5-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics. This approach, however, oversimplifies the complex dynamics of a highly distorted neutron star in an expanding disk. To address this limitation, we have developed a new method that applies a shared envelope (SE) framework, which recognizes the overlap between the neutron star and the disk. This approach uses a more comprehensive set of equations that incorporate the distortions of the neutron star and the disk's surface, allowing for a more accurate calculation of the disk's density and the neutron star's surface location. This method enhances our understanding of the neutron star's interaction with the disk, leading to a new expression for its energy generation due to friction, which is often the dominant energy source in this process. This new energy generation mechanism is typically negative, indicating that energy is released from the disk to the neutron star. This, in turn, leads to the star's surface expanding at a rate faster than the disk, resulting in a more dramatic effect on their interaction. Furthermore, this new approach results in the neutron star's surface location shifting further away from the center, causing its surface to expand more significantly. This, in turn, reduces the density of the neutron star's surface, leading to a smaller mass transfer rate. This new method also leads to the discovery of a critical initial separation distance between the neutron star and the black hole, above which the neutron star's surface will be entirely engulfed by the disk, making this system unsuitable for producing an electromagnetic signal associated with this process. This emergent behavior is directly linked to the SE framework and will continue to influence the neutron star's dynamics even after its breakup, primarily due to the release of its gravitational potential energy as it interacts with the disk. This new approach results in the release of the neutron star's internal energy at a slower rate than previously estimated, leading to a smaller total energy release. This, in turn, reduces the maximum energy released from the neutron star's breakup, which is now lower than previously predicted. This new method also allows for a more comprehensive comparison with numerical simulations that incorporate a more detailed neutron star physics, revealing small discrepancies in the density distribution of the neutron star

This research presents new findings from the second generation of observations at the Plateosaurus field in the Chandra Legacy program, focusing on five Seyfert galaxies (Mrk 1, Mrk 331, Mrk 348, Mrk 573, and Mrk 1066). Our study reveals ionized gas outside the direction of ionization in the nuclei of Mrk 1066 and Mrk 573. These features, located about 7.5 kiloparsecs from the galaxies' centers, exhibit the same velocity as the main ionized gas components and are likely the result of gas interacting with fast galaxy outflows. Additionally, Mrk 573 shows a larger, more extended ionized gas region with velocities indicating a 300-kilometer-per-second difference between its edges, possibly due to gas being compressed by an incoming shock. This discovery provides evidence for shock waves producing new emission in galaxy outflows. Furthermore, a previously undetected ionized gas component in Mrk 1 may be associated with a reflected shock wave, while Mrk 331 and Mrk 348 display ionized gas with velocities consistent with their host galaxies' rotation curves. Our study highlights the importance of optical observations and spectral lines for understanding the physics of gas outflows. Optimizing the design of future X-ray observations with spatial resolution is also crucial for making the most of upcoming large-scale surveys of active galaxies. This is because the relatively low flux of bright Seyfert galaxies may limit the effectiveness of optimized observations. Our results also suggest that gas outflows are a common feature in Seyfert galaxies and may be more widespread than previously thought. This has implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution, as outflows may significantly impact the distribution of gas and stars within galaxies. Furthermore, the relationship between active galactic nuclei and their host galaxies requires further study, and the ionized gas component in Mrk 573, which shows a connection between the galaxy's central black hole and its massive star stream, is a key target for such research. However, manually creating realistic scenes through traditional methods such as 3D modeling and editing is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. To streamline this process and automate scene generation, machine learning-based approaches can be tailored to produce high-quality scenes using training data. Despite the numerous applications for traffic scenes in the field of computer vision, there is a shortage of public datasets suitable for training models to generate realistic scenes through multiple stages. To bridge this gap, we introduce SceneGen, a comprehensive traffic scene generation platform that divides the scene creation process into multiple stages and trains separate models for each one. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that have limited period lengths - specifically those that are greater than 2. These measures aren't just periodic but also maintain an average with any given degree on the tree. We demonstrate that these measures are mixtures of periodic measures that are closely tied to the measures found on a binary tree. The model includes a non-density-dependent birth process and a death process that is influenced by the population's presence. To control the population, we introduce a precisely placed and timed source term. Our goal is to determine whether this control can eliminate the population over a finite period. Our analysis accounts for various sizes and locations of the subpopulations. Notably, we demonstrate that complete controllability can be achieved in a subdomain of two dimensions, providing a practical application of a Carleman estimate in the context of partial differential equations. However, in domains of more complex geometry, we establish conditions under which controllability can be achieved in cases where the model exhibits a strong distinction between growing and dying components. Additionally, we explore scenarios where these components exhibit similar dynamics, and we identify a size condition related to the model's reproduction number that distinguishes controllable and non-controllable scenarios. A key aspect of our study is the derivation of a subdomain-based approach to estimating solutions of the population dynamics equation. This approach enables us to formulate an optimal control problem and analyze its existence and uniqueness. Finally, we discuss an extension of the model that includes a reaction term and its implications for controllability. Additionally, we provide a numerical solution technique based on a backward solver and demonstrate its effectiveness with numerical experiments. These experiments involve a model with a reaction term and highlight the distinction between growing and dying components in relation to the model's dynamics. Furthermore, we observe that in scenarios where the model's density-dependent death term becomes non-monotonic, the model exhibits a persistence phenomenon. In soccer, the final outcome is determined by achieving scoring opportunities, which can be challenging to create in limited time with only a few players on the field. Our research focuses on suggesting tactics for both teams to increase their chances of scoring or preventing the opposing team from scoring, utilizing a limited number of players over a short period. We've developed a unique state representation, reinforced learning algorithms, and evaluation metrics to test our approach's effectiveness. Our results show that, in scenarios with only a few players left on the field, our proposed strategy leads to a higher scoring probability than the standard 4-4-2 formation. However, as more players rejoin the game, the standard formation becomes more advantageous. To better understand these findings, we analyzed the distribution of players on the field and identified situations where our team was more likely to score or prevent the opposing team from scoring. These insights could be applied to develop more comprehensive soccer game algorithms. Our research used the soccer game simulation environment developed by Shirokov et al. and implemented an adaptive agent architecture advised by the results obtained. The basis of optical nonreversibility in quantum-dotted semiconductors remains poorly understood due to the intricate interplay of light, matter, and the reverse process driven by photon-phonon interactions. A new mechanism, involving the collapse of a quantum state as light interacts with the semiconductor, is proposed to explain this phenomenon. This mechanism, demonstrated through time-domain electroluminescence, enables optical nonreversibility and amplifies the impact of a single quantum dot over 10,000-fold. As a result, this discovery may facilitate the development of more efficient light sources and optical switches. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of photon-phonon interactions in semiconductors, a factor that current theories fail to account for, and suggests a new method for evaluating the quantum state of semiconductors. This approach may also be applied to other semiconductors, such as those with loose boundaries, and could provide a way to control the propagation of quantum information. This discovery is particularly significant in the field of quantum communication, where secure transmission relies on the preservation of a quantum state over long distances. Although there are methods to protect quantum states from environmental influences, there is currently no solution for protecting them during transmission. This issue needs to be addressed before quantum communication can be implemented over extended paths. One approach to resolving this challenge involves using the phenomenon of spontaneous emission in semiconductors to create a situation where the quantum state of a single photon is influenced by the presence of many other photons. This results in the emission of a new photon with different properties, such as a change in its polarization or the frequency at which it oscillates. This process can be controlled by adjusting the properties of the semiconductor and can be used to transmit data over long distances. However, this method is not efficient and a large amount of light is required to create the necessary conditions, making it difficult to implement over extended paths. Moreover, the process is not precise and the properties of the emitted photon are not consistent, which creates difficulties in receiving the transmitted data. To overcome these limitations, researchers are exploring ways to use a different property of light, known as its entanglement, to transmit data. This involves creating a situation where the quantum state of a single photon is connected to the state of many other photons, a phenomenon that can be influenced by the presence of a single quantum dot. Although this method shows promise, it is a complex process and there are many variables that need to be controlled, which makes it difficult to implement over long distances.

On November 7, 2019, IGR J19294+1816, which had been inactive since 2009, emerged as the top source in the sky above 10 keV. It demonstrated its energy spectrum and temporal behavior during a flare, exhibiting a cyclotron absorption feature and a quasi-periodical oscillation. To further investigate, the Maxwellian distribution temperature increased from 13.5 to 18.4 keV and the oscillation period rose from 577 ms to 599 ms. A detailed analysis of these parameters was conducted using the data from the spectroscopic and timing instruments on board the AstroSat. Additionally, the absence of a significant tail below 10 keV in the spectrum during the 2019 flare season set it apart from the 2010 outburst. This unique characteristic, combined with the source's low galactic column density, suggested that the cyclotron line and the oscillation pattern observed during the 2019 flare likely originated from the accretion column in an intermediate magnetic field strength neutron star. Furthermore, the observed mHz QPO in IGR J19294+1816 provided valuable insights into its intermediately strong magnetic field, making it the second known example of such a phenomenon. This discovery left the possibility open that there may be more neutron stars with similar properties, awaiting identification. Additionally, the fact that IGR J19294+1816 displayed its highest energy emission since its discovery also highlighted the sensitivity of MAXI, which often locates new transient sources and mark their most intense moments. However, it also left room for other instruments like AstroSat to uncover more intricate details during these events. Lastly, the detection of a cyclotron line and oscillations in IGR J19294+1816 provided scientists with a unique opportunity to study the physics of neutron stars over extended periods, up to a week, which is crucial in furthering their understanding of these celestial bodies. This study was conducted when the primary detector on board the Astrosat, the Sky Map, was non-functional, using the remaining detectors and demonstrating that even without the primary detector, the on board instruments can collect valuable information. A recent variant of the voter model, featuring a competition-colonization tradeoff, has been examined for its dynamics on a biologically relevant timescale. This model includes two types of species with distinct characteristics: species with high colonization rates and low competition against other individuals of the same species, and species with low colonization rates and strong competition against other individuals of the same species. This study focuses on a chaotic version of the model, where species are distributed uniformly across a closed spatial domain. Results show that the model exhibits a critical point at a colonization rate equal to the rate of death due to competition, and that this critical point determines whether a specific species will become extinct or coexist with the other species. Furthermore, proof demonstrates that the model's phase space crosses from a state where one species dominates to a state where the other species dominates through a homoclinic orbit. Additionally, the model exhibits a higher degree of stability at the critical point, and this stability is achieved at a colonization rate that is half of the rate at which strong competition causes death, which is consistent with models representing the evolution of species. Finally, the model's behavior can be modified to represent species with intermediate characteristics by incorporating a competition-colonization tradeoff, which results in the emergence of a three-dimensional phase space that allows for the coexistence of all species. It also shows that the critical factor determining the outcome is the relative ratio of these rates, and that this result holds true in a chaotic environment. Continuous speech synthesis offers a comprehensive speech generation solution, yet existing methods typically isolate each sentence from previous ones. However, natural conversations often demand a deeper understanding of the larger context. To address this limitation, a novel context-aware synthesis approach called MaskedDialogue is proposed, integrating a masking technique to leverage contextual cues. By masking part of the generated text in each sentence, a cross-entropy loss is introduced to ensure the coherence of the overall paragraph. Our proposed system is tested on not only single-sentence datasets but also various conversation datasets. Experimental results indicate that MaskedDialogue achieves superior performance compared to baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating contextual aspects in speech synthesis. Moreover, a lack of lattice-based guidance in previous data augmentation methods like Masked RNN leads to synthesis of less natural sentences, further confirming the superiority of MaskedDialogue. Our model's ability to grasp contextual meaning also enables it to generate more accurate summaries of conversations. To facilitate model training, a simple yet efficient interaction-based mechanism is introduced, reducing the need for complicated pre-training and fine-tuning processes. Implementing this approach yields high-quality samples in various evaluation metrics, along with engaging audio content. Our code and model are publicly available for access. Despite achieving top performance, MaskedDialogue remains a relatively simple model with limited parameters, indicating vast room for improvement through the exploration of advanced features and architectures. To this end, possible directions for future research in this context are also outlined. Our results specifically demonstrate substantial gains in conversational datasets, amounting to 31.57% higher metrics scores on L100 test sets, and show that even small improvements in single-sentence synthesis models translate to significant gains in conversational settings. Our study highlights the significance of developing context-aware synthesis models that can effectively utilize contextual cues to produce more accurate and engaging speech. To this end, I am pleased to present our context-aware synthesis model, MaskedDialogue, which has shown superior performance in single-sentence and conversation datasets over popular baseline models like Transformer, Improved Transformer, Transformer-XL, and BART. A strong connection between van Hove singularities and the formation of pseudogaps has been a longstanding hypothesis in solid-state physics. Recently, lattice models exhibiting both van Hove behavior and pseudogaps have been developed, albeit rarely in one-dimensional systems. Building upon Aberdeen Tunnel's unique under-ice research facility, we propose a design for a device that can monitor spallation neutrons produced when cosmic muons interact with ice. This device is comprised of three layers of plastic-scintillator detectors, arranged perpendicular to one another to cover periphery and central areas. It is capable of detecting muon bundles and counting spallation neutrons generated from muon interactions with ice. Furthermore, by tracking the production rates of these neutrons, we can develop a reference point for future experiments focusing on neutrino research. Additionally, to validate our device's design, we performed simulations using realistic representations of Aberdeen Tunnel's environment and the scintillator materials. These simulations indicated that our design can achieve an accuracy within 6% when measuring spallation neutron production rates. We believe that our device design is not only applicable to Aberdeen Tunnel but also has implications for similar under-ice research facilities. We are in the process of constructing the actual device in our laboratory and plan to perform preliminary data validation before its deployment at Aberdeen Tunnel. If successful, we aim to incorporate a liquid-scintillator tank into the design to further enhance its functionality. We welcome feedback and collaboration with fellow researchers in this field.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect (YORP) causes a net torque on asteroids, leading to a change in their rotation velocity. In a study of three asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, the YORP influence was calculated and a range of possible values was estimated for each asteroid. While (10115) 1992 SK's short observation period prevents conclusive YORP measurements, (1685) Toro and (1620) Geographos showed significant increases in their rotation velocities, with an estimated time frame of around 10 million years for both asteroids to complete one rotation in less than 2 days. Additionally, (1620) Geographos displays a prograde rotation, which is unusual among large asteroids that tend to have retrograde rotations. The YORP effect is most effective in its influence on asteroids with irregular shapes, particularly those with a low equatorial velocity. As a result, (1685) Toro and (1620) Geographos are likely to continue experiencing increased rotation velocities, with (1620) Geographos potentially becoming one of the fastest rotating asteroids in the future. The study's findings highlight the significant impact of the YORP effect on asteroids and its important role in shaping their rotation characteristics. The study's results also suggest that (10115) 1992 SK may have a substantial YORP effect and could experience a significant rise in its rotation velocity in the future. By analyzing comments left by voters under posts made by politicians, we can gain insight into the underlying dynamics of their conversations. However, there is a lack of understanding regarding the cointeraction networks that govern these discussions. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of voter comments on the accounts of Indian politicians during the 2019 Indian General Election. Utilizing a custom-made algorithm to identify relevant co-interactions, we extracted co-interaction triples from 4500 posts made by 18 politicians, resulting in a dataset comprising 157 million voters and featuring distinct temporal activity patterns. Furthermore, we observed that politicians with greater following counts tend to spark more active discussions, but struggle to sustain engagement over time. Moreover, we discovered that voters' participation exhibits seasonal fluctuations, peaking during election day and showing a clear diurnal pattern with increased activity in the evening. To further explore these findings, we developed two new measures of influence, namely, co-temporal reach and co-temporal impact, which provide a temporal perspective on a voter's ability to initiate and contribute to discussions. We found that voters exhibiting these patterns are often re-elected and tend to maintain a strong online presence. Additionally, we identified three primary topics of discussion, namely, development, corruption, and nationalism, which receive consistent attention from voters, with some voters consistently contributing to these topics and demonstrating a sense of leadership within the online community. To better explore the temporal aspects of these co-interaction networks, we conducted a dynamic network perspective analysis, which reveals that the underlying structure of these discussions evolves over time, with changes occurring every few days. We observed that some voters exhibit a sense of persistence, consistently contributing to discussions across various topics, while others prefer to focus on a single topic. Furthermore, we found that voters with a broader online presence tend to exhibit persistence more frequently. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the co-interaction networks that govern political conversations on Instagram, with implications for politicians seeking to engage with voters through online discussions. To achieve this, we offer a perspective that emphasizes the importance of persistently contributing to discussions on various topics, with a focus on building a sense of community and leadership online. This is particularly crucial during election campaigns, with voters placing a high value on politicians with a strong online presence and a history of initiating and sustaining discussions. Although M-dwarfs exhibit many characteristics similar to G-dwarfs, their UV spectra are significantly affected by molecular absorption, primarily from CH and CN species, which are formed through stellar atmospheric processes. As a result, standard calibration methods used for G-dwarfs are less effective for M-dwarfs, necessitating a novel approach to calculate their physical properties. By utilizing a large data set of 89 M-dwarf UV spectra, our algorithm calculates the equivalent widths of multiple spectral lines, which are then used in combinations to estimate the stellar parameters through a non-linear least squares method. This process is highly automated, enabling the analysis of a large number of M-dwarf spectra. As part of the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Collection, this study presents the calculated stellar parameters for 89 field M-dwarfs, spanning from early A to late M spectral types, and includes a spectral type-spectral line relation for all major elements formed through stellar atmospheric processes. This approach is highly useful for any observational or theoretical project involving M-dwarfs, including the search for exoplanets, studying their rotation periods, or analyzing the composition of their atmospheres. A key aspect of this definition is the requirement that the operation's application to any two infinite strings can be computably determined, including in cases where the strings' common prefix does not influence the resulting infinite string. A notable property of computable operations is that they generate an order-preserving order on the set of computable infinite strings, enabling the solution of various computability-related problems. A further development involves a computable total order that can be derived from any computable operation, and this is demonstrated to result in a computably finite number of distinct infinite strings with computably interwoven substrings. For second-order dynamic games under information asymmetry, we develop a new method for determining achievable sets that maintains a Cauchy-type form. This method relies on solving a novel variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enabling the identification of the maximum or minimum set subject to a given target set and constraint. Unlike existing methods, our approach assumes no explicit expression for the opponent's control, instead utilizing the existence of a continuous feedback solution for sub-optimal play. Building on our new method, we also establish conditions for determining the smallest or largest controllable/controllable-at-worst set within a given achievable set, forming a Cauchy-type structure. However, we point out that these conditions may not be necessary, as illustrated through a counterexample. Nonetheless, our approach provides a valuable framework for analyzing the controllability or controllability-at-worst of sets in games under asymmetric information, as demonstrated through the examination of a related problem of set reachability. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the design of stabilizable regions of games under information asymmetry, as they provide insights into the construction of asymptotically stable sets through the application of the Cauchy-type method for achievable sets computation. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential extensions and areas for further research in this area.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, the ability to generalize across tasks unaided remains a key aspect of human intelligence. This study aims to investigate a similar concept in machines: the ability to generalize across tasks without guidance. We define this capability as the ability to successfully perform a task (referred to as the 'target' task) on the basis of their performance in other related tasks (the'source' tasks). To demonstrate the existence of this capability in machines, we utilize a publicly available dataset that comprises diverse text classification tasks. By applying an unsupervised learning approach to the dataset's existing labeled data, we enhance the performance of multiple unseen target tasks through a combination of selective attention to relevant source tasks. Our results show superior performance when comparing machines with this unservised capability to those without it. Moreover, we observe that the attention mechanism plays a crucial role in achieving this capability. To further validate this capability in machines, we introduce an alternative method that eliminates the need for labeled data in the source tasks while still achieving comparable performance. These findings provide tangible evidence for the existence of the capability to generalize across tasks without guidance and offer practical solutions that are both effective and efficient. Additionally, they highlight multiple potential applications for this capability, including the development of simple models that can generalize across large numbers of tasks while also facilitating the exploration of new tasks without the need for labeled data. All of this contributes significantly to the ongoing quest to develop machines that are more like humans in their ability to generalize across tasks. This research is a preliminary step in a broader area of study that involves investigating various aspects of the capability to generalize across tasks without guidance while also exploring new methods for its implementation. In our research, we focused on resolving two key challenges in the implementation of differential privacy in machine learning: the lack of a clear understanding of how private models can be optimized for better performance, and the limited consideration given to hyperparameter tuning in training private models. Our experiments revealed that the performance of private neural networks is significantly inferior to their non-private counterparts, and this decline grows more pronounced as the training data decreases. To mitigate this issue, we developed a hyperparameter tuning framework for differential privacy in deep learning, which leverages a distortion-based algorithm to identify optimal hyperparameters that balance performance and privacy concerns. Our findings show that this approach yields private models with improved accuracy, and the gain in performance is further enhanced when the training data increases. Notably, our method exhibits advantages over existing practices, and our experiments across multiple classification tasks and varying dataset sizes provide insight into the optimal hyperparameters for training private models. Our research provides a foundation for investigating ways to enhance the performance of private machine learning models. In addition, we introduced a new benchmark focused on differential privacy in deep learning, which can be found at https://github.com/anti-tank-gun/private-baselines. This benchmark enables the straightforward evaluation of various private learning methods and allows for explorations of how to balance performance and privacy. It is applicable to leading deep learning datasets and readily extensible to incorporate new datasets. This research paper proposes an stream processing engine called LifeStream, 
which is designed to efficiently manage periodic data flows. Unlike traditional 
stream processing systems that focus on handling individual events, LifeStream 
is optimized for systems that repeatedly process the same type of data at fixed 
intervals. We've developed a new concept called "window-in-motion" to help 
understand how data evolves over time and created a unique approach to 
processing periodic data, combining sorting and scanning techniques. Furthermore, 
we've implemented a number of optimizations, including precomputing and 
caching, to minimize processing time. Our experiments show that LifeStream can 
achieve significant performance improvements over other stream processing systems, 
with improvements of up to 5 times for certain workloads. However, the paper 
also identifies certain limitations with current data management systems, leading 
to potential research directions in the field. LifeStream has been made 
open-source and is now available for use. 

In the first part of the paper, we discuss the underlying principles and design 
decisions behind LifeStream. We then move on to presenting the performance 
evaluations of LifeStream, comparing it to other stream processing systems. 

The system is composed of three main modules: the scheduler, the operator layer 
and the storage layer. We've chosen to use a sorted array for data storage and 
developed an in-memory index to locate specific data segments. The scheduler is 
responsible for managing the processing of data segments and ensuring that they 
are processed in the correct order. The operator layer contains the actual 
processing components, such as the sort and scan operators. 

In terms of storage, LifeStream uses an array that is sorted by a primary key, 
with each data entry consisting of an ID, a value and a timestamp. The index, 
on the other hand, is an unsorted array containing only the IDs of the data 
entries. When processing a new data segment, LifeStream first determines the 
relevant data entries by performing a binary search with the index, before 
switching to a linear search to locate any adjacent data entries that may also 
be relevant. 

The performance evaluations were conducted on a machine with 4 cores and 64 GB of RAM, using a dataset of 64 million entries with a retention period of 50 hours. The results show that LifeStream achieves the best performance, with processing times of up to 5 times better than other systems.

One of the key challenges in teaching robots via positive reinforcement learning is ensuring they understand what behaviors are desired. To overcome this limitation, it's possible to train robots using corrective guidance, which informs them about desired actions through what they observe other agents doing. However, the current methods for doing so rely on specific details of the task environment, which hinders their potential for broad application. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that allows robots to learn from a wide range of corrective guidance sources, regardless of the type of task they're performing, as long as it involves interacting with physical objects using grasping and manipulating. This meta-algorithm demonstrates its effectiveness in teaching robots to accomplish diverse tasks via just a few demonstrations and learns even more efficiently when given more corrective feedback. Notably, it excels particularly in situations where the provided feedback is accurate, which isn't always the case in real-world applications. To train robots using corrective guidance, we also develop multiple sources of challenging tasks that involve complex manipulation tasks and test our meta-algorithm on them, proving that its ability to learn from such data extends to a broader class of tasks requiring both vision and motor skills. This work provides a significant breakthrough in using a broad-based learning approach for teaching robots via positive reinforcement, but it doesn't address another crucial aspect - safety, which isn't considered in this research. This paper is being presented at the 2022 Robotics: Science and Systems Conference.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes self-supervised optimization of policies that prioritize clusters of optimal actions, as defined by transition dynamics. Formulating an optimized policy using this approach involves computing the stationary distribution of transition dynamics, which can be challenging due to its computation-intensive nature. In contrast, our proposed framework, CRRNet, leverages visual representations of state distributions to circumvent this computation, as it assumes states are embedded in a metric space represented by a Euclidean projection. Through the use of state-to-embedding mappings, as well as the use of interpolation techniques, we demonstrate that visually aided cluster ranking provides a more efficient and versatile framework for reward learning, as it significantly reduces computational demands and allows for the learning of policies in multiple settings. Experimental results show that our proposed method achieves comparable performance to optimized baselines and outperforms existing techniques using state-to-embedding mappings. Furthermore, CRRNet exhibits superior performance in multi-task learning scenarios. In particular, we show that it is highly effective in learning policies for a complex kitchen task, as well as its individual sub-tasks. Source code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/chenchen-1990/Time-Effective-RL. In comparison to baseline policies that compute the stationary distribution through policy evaluation, our method achieves similar performance but at a tiny fraction of the memory required.
