Recently, a team of researchers suggested a link between personality and prescription drug use, suggesting that personality could predict individuals prone to misusing medications. Notably, these predictions were based on a reduced version of the Five Factor Model, excluding the 'openness' dimension, and focused on individuals who had been diagnosed with substance abuse or had family histories of abuse. The results support the link between the full Five Factor Model and prescription drug use, revealing specific drug utilization risk profiles for distinct personality traits. Conversely, those with high agreeableness were less likely to be prescribed these types of medications. To date, there is a lack of comprehensive datasets that capture these types of logical connections, which are fundamental to if-then reasoning and universally accepted across different cultures.  To address this gap, we have assembled a diverse group of native English speakers representing different age groups and geographical regions.  They evaluated existing datasets, labeled examples, and collaborated to establish best practices for identifying causal links in texts.  Our dataset comprises nearly a million entries, which include over 20,000 if-then reasoning rules.  To facilitate further research into these rules, we have developed multiple related datasets that include complementary information such as causal links between objects, potential responses to instances of these rules, and related emotional states.  Our results show that current machine learning models struggle to predict future events based on established connections and that there is significant room for improvement in areas like minimalism, where less information yields more accurate outcomes.  By achieving better performance on tasks involving these rule-based connections, we have demonstrated gains in related areas such as natural language understanding and emotional recognition.  Our paper presents an in-depth analysis of these findings and proposes innovative approaches for tackling these challenges through machine learning.  We believe that sharing our datasets, models, and evaluation protocols will facilitate further research into these essential logical connections and facilitate their integration into various applications requiring emotional intelligence, such as human-human and human-machine interfaces, personal assistants, and recommendations.  We have made all the code, models, and data available at https://github.com/originv2/atomic and look forward to collaborating with the research community on this vital area. This method involves training two models in parallel: a speech model that predicts a probability distribution over words and a text model that generates the speech data. The speech model is further modified to include a bidirectional attention mechanism, allowing it to focus on both relevant speech features and the accompanying text. Experimental results show that our proposed approach outperforms traditional multi-modal training methods and achieves comparable performance to that of models pre-trained on vast amounts of data. Notably, our method enables the integration of additional data in the form of text alone, enabling further reduction of the speech recognition word error rate. A uniform parking function can be visualized as a point (x,y) within a unit square, where x and y represent the numbers of passes made by the first and second players in a fair game, respectively. This concept is closely related to the order polytope, a geometric object that has received significant study in the field of combinatorial geometry. As the number of elements within the ordered set grows larger, an interesting phenomenon emerges, where the initial positions of the points (x,y) form a shape that converges to a specific asymptotic form. This paper delves into the detailed examination of this geometric object and provides numerical values for the measures of its convexity. It also offers insights into the underlying reasons for the asymmetry observed in the points (x,y) and discusses the implications of this asymmetry, as well as the effects it has on the order polytope itself. Additionally, this paper introduces the term "shifted ladder system" to describe a particular configuration related to the points (x,y) and presents evidence that this configuration is, in fact, a building block of the order polytope. Furthermore, this paper establishes an interesting connection between the points (x,y) and those (y,x), and it also explores the notion of "symmetric uniform parking functions." Lastly, this paper raises an important question regarding the relationship between the points (x,y) and those (y,x), and it provides numerical values for the number of symmetric uniform parking functions that correspond to the highest level within the lattice structure. This value serves as a significant component in the calculation of the convex hull of random symmetric order polytopes. It is essential to note that the points (y,x) form a shape that converges to a different asymptotic form, and while this form is known, the detailed examination of its measures is currently underway. Moreover, this paper establishes that the shifted ladder system, which is unique to the points (x,y), is not present in the points (y,x). Lastly, this paper raises the question of whether the points (x,y) and those (y,x) will eventually converge to the same form as the number of elements within the ordered set continues to increase. This is a novel contribution to the study of symmetric order polytopes, and it is anticipated that further research in this area will be an exciting and rewarding pursuit. In quantum key distribution, a crucial process called measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) is considered the most secure way to generate secret keys, leveraging the quantum principle of linear channel attenuation to detect malicious behavior of the communication network. However, there is a significant limitation to implementing MDI-QKD over extended distances - it requires the use of entangled resource, which drastically reduces the length of generated keys. To overcome this hurdle, researchers have proposed converting classical key generation into a quantum process called quantum backwards reconciliation, utilizing classical source coding and involving all parties in the communication network. Notably, this conversion enables the use of classical reconciliation instead of quantum state merging, the original process used in QKD. As such, it allows key generation in noisy channels without the need for entangled resources. Although this modification allows key generation in noisy channels, it introduces the risk of malicious behavior by network participants. To detect such tampering, researchers have proposed incorporating an additively white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel and developed a novel demonstration of the security of this modified process. The proposed demonstration relies on the unique characteristics of Gaussian distributions to distinguish malicious behavior and maintains the same success rate in demonstrating the security of MDI-QKD, even when the amount of noise in the communication network is increased. Furthermore, this demonstration reduces the accuracy of channel estimation but still successfully identify the attack in up to 95% of cases. Notably, this reduction in accuracy does not result in the duplication of the shared secret, as it occurs rarely enough. Nonetheless, this proposal may be vulnerable to a novel attack that allows the detection of the measurement basis attack in exchange for a small decrease in the density of noise in the communication network. Although this attack is detectable in the demonstration, it still presents an interesting consideration for extending the length of generated keys in MDI-QKD over extended distances. To address this issue, researchers may consider implementing a novel modulation scheme that converts the measurement device independent encoding used in MDI-QKD into a key generation process that is secure against malicious behavior by network participants, allowing the use of entangled resources without reducing the length of generated keys. This novel modulation scheme maintains the same success rate in demonstrating the security of MDI-QKD when the amount of noise in the communication network is increased and reduces the required noise in the Gaussian distribution by up to 50%. Furthermore, it increases the ratio of information carrying capacity to the required entangled resources in up to 95% of cases, significantly enhancing the potential of MDI-QKD

The spin-orbit proximity effect, where a strong spin-orbit coupling present in one material influences the spin dynamics of another, has been extensively explored for its potential to increase spin-polarization and rotation frequency in molecular magnets.  Investigating this phenomenon is complex due to the interplay between various factors such as proximity scattering, carrier mobility, and boundary scattering.  Our study focuses on the electrical transport properties of Bi/Co multilayer films as they exhibit both proximity proximity effect and edge effect.  According to our results, the presence of a strong spin-orbit coupling in the Bi film causes a skew scattering process that counteracts the spin-orbit proximity effect, leading to a decrease in the anomalous Hall conductivity.  Conversely, the grain boundary scattering dominates the normal Hall conductivity, resulting in an increase that eventually overcomes the proximity effect's decline.  Consequently, choice of film with appropriate grain size becomes essential for realizing the spin-orbit proximity effect.  Moreover, our findings are relevant to research on Bi-based proximitized ferromagnetic superconductors where edge scattering may influence the critical current density.  Consequently, there is a need for a systematic investigation of these effects that may facilitate device optimization.  Our study also demonstrates that the edge scattering-dominated transport can be manipulated by altering the Bi film's thickness, an unexplored means of controlling this effect that holds promise for its application in spin-orbit coupled systems.  Our research indicates that the spin-orbit proximity effect can be optimized through film thickness modification, a discovery that may be extended to other overlap scenarios.  Our results, which show the strong influence of edge scattering on the proximitized electrons, may provide a basis for understanding similar phenomena in graphene and cadmium arsenide based systems.  Furthermore, this knowledge may be utilized to modify the spin-orbit coupling in these systems through the variation of edge scattering.  Our findings also highlight the complexity involved in understanding the spin-orbit proximity effect that arises due to the simultaneous presence of proximity scattering, carrier mobility, and boundary scattering. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental limitations in my opinion.
I believe recent successes are primarily driven by the availability of vast amounts of data rather than any inherent advantage.
I further speculate that simple linear models would still outperform sequential models when data is scarce.
To support this claim, I conducted an experiment using the BERT model and a linear regression baseline to determine which one performed better on the Basque Treebank. The results showed that although BERT model performed better, a linear model with sufficient training data could achieve comparable performance. To address this, I trained a linear model on the Basque Treebank and compared it to a neural network model with the same number of parameters. However, the neural network model failed to learn from the data and performed significantly worse than the linear model. To overcome this challenge, I trained both models on the same dataset but with a different structure, and surprisingly, the neural network model performed significantly better when the dependency labels were predicted simultaneously with the part-of-speech tags. This finding highlights the importance of modeling the co-occurrence of dependent words when predicting syntactic dependencies. The models I trained achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on the test set but still performed below the standards set by state-of-the-art systems that employ sequence-to-sequence models. I also explored the ability of these models to generalize to unseen data and observed that although they performed well on the test set, they struggled to generalize to sentences with longer dependency distances. To overcome this limitation, I trained a linear model with a different structure that was able to generalize to sentences with dependency distances over 5. Despite achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the Basque Treebank, the models I trained struggled with the English Treebank, a dataset with less aggressive pruning. This difficulty was attributed to the models' limited ability to capture the dependencies in such sentences. To address this challenge, I trained a linear model on the English Treebank with a different structure that was able to generalize to sentences with dependency distances over 5. This model performed significantly better than a neural network model with the same number of parameters and achieved state-of-the-art accuracy on the test set. This improvement was primarily driven by the models' ability to capture the agreements in such sentences. To validate this, I conducted an analysis of the parameters of both models. This occurrence allows for a precise determination of the planet's cross-sectional area as it moves within one millionth of a square degree of visibility. Its highly elliptical 111.4-day orbit makes its star-shading phenomenon a brief one, lasting only 48 hours. HD80606b's interaction with its star's gravitational field causes a significant daily tug on the planet, resulting in about 120 km of orbital velocity. Although this orbital velocity should generate considerable wind turbulence on the planet, observations during a similar close approach did not detect any associated stellar energy absorption beyond expected levels, suggesting the planet's atmospheric capacity may be relatively low, possibly due to its massive nature. Its gravitational pull causes a permanent 0.5km/s wind flow on the side of the planet facing the star. HD80606b's close approach to its star will be observable from the ground for about 48 hours on each of four days in June and July 2023, with some data likely useful for further analysis with the launch of JWST. Systemic corrections during these events may allow for a more accurate determination of the planet's orbital parameters and any existing tidal heating it may experience. Additionally, observations of the planet's light during these close approaches may be used to identify variations in its atmospheric conditions and potential wind flow effects on the light observed. In rehabilitative games, artificial intelligence models monitor a patient's performance to adjust the level of difficulty, but they typically focus on virtual environments. By incorporating a simulation-based framework for neural network control, we can apply this concept to physical rehabilitation across various activities, ensuring that models accurately account for a patient's physical limitations and adapt to their skills in real-time. This hybrid approach combines simulated predictions with actual sensor data to guide the game's difficulty level and provides visual feedback to both the patient and the therapist. We demonstrated our method's effectiveness in two experiments, one with a simulated patient whose performance matched the predicted outcomes from the model, and the other with a real patient who showed improved performance after playing the rehabilitative game with our system. Our method has the potential to make rehabilitative games more engaging and challenging for patients, but it requires further exploration of its long-term benefits. We are currently investigating the integration of our system with advanced machine learning algorithms to make it even more suitable for a wider range of patients and activities. We are open to collaborations and are releasing our code and a demonstration of our program publicly. This paper investigates the link between CT and modern coreference resolution systems, seeking to answer how these systems, driven by neural networks, manage coherence. To this end, the paper introduces a new metric called coherence score based on CT, which assesses the naturalness of associated pairs in the data used to train coreference models. The results of the experiments indicate that these models are able to capture the coherence implied by the structural relationships between sentences automatically, without the need for additional features. Furthermore, the paper finds that there is a correlation between the coherence implied by the data and the coherence actually observed in the associated pairs, revealing that coreference resolution systems can already handle coherence effectively. To build on this, the paper introduces a method for training coreference resolution systems that prioritize coherence, using the CT-based metric as a target. The evaluation of the models produced reveals that they perform similarly to the current state-of-the-art systems, while also exhibiting improved coherence in the predicted outputs. We investigate new parameters that guarantee an upward-planar representation of weighted directed graphs, specifically focusing on the minimum number of source vertices and the maximum out-degree across all vertices. Notably, we find that a graph is upward-planar if it has no source vertices and a maximum out-degree of two, but this condition is not sufficient for a graph with no source vertices to be upward-planar. Nevertheless, we identify that a graph with no source vertices and a maximum out-degree of three for some vertices is upward-planar, and this inequality cannot be relaxed. To demonstrate this, we also derive a simple algorithm for identifying whether a graph with no source vertices and a maximum out-degree of three for some vertices has an upward-planar representation, and this problem becomes NP-complete when the degree constraint is increased to four. Moreover, we present a generalized framework for converting an upward-planar drawing into a upward-surface-planar drawing, and this involves removing edges from the original graph. Notably, this removal strategy is applicable to classes of graphs that have the ability to exclude certain subgraphs, and this is explicitly demonstrated with graphs that have the ability to exclude $K_4$ and series-parallel graphs. Finally, we discuss an open problem related to finding the smallest integer that guarantees an graph to be upward-planar. We introduce a new framework that allows an AI to manage role-playing games by leading players through scenarios, making decisions, and resolving conflicts. Based on the principles of these games, we develop a set of characters, rules, and story elements that can be learned from descriptions found on the official D&D website. To effectively lead the game, we train an AI to understand the intentions and thoughts of players, giving it a limited form of Theory-of-Mind. By giving the AI access to a wide range of game states and being able to express its decisions in a natural way, we demonstrate that it can create an engaging and coherent game experience. Additionally, we discover that adding a simple mechanism of predication enables the AI to create more complex story developments, leading to a more satisfying player experience. And finally, we show that this approach can also be applied to other interactive storytelling platforms. By testing our framework against human players and comparing the opinions of multiple Dungeon Masters, we validate that the games produced by the AI are enjoyable and meet the standards of experienced players. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, the field remains underdeveloped. This study introduces a novel approach to address this gap by focusing on identifying semantic shifts in word meanings. Distinguishing this approach from existing methods, our proposed technique does not compare the meaning of words over time, instead it analyzes how the meanings of words evolve in response to each other. To achieve this, we introduce a new model that represents word meanings as interacting low-dimensional vectors. These vectors enable us to pinpoint words that exhibit semantic shifts by detecting the existing semantic relationships they were once a part of but no longer are. Existing methods for change detection are outperformed by our proposed approach, and it holds particular value in areas like semantic-based stock market analysis and medical diagnosis. However, it faces challenges when dealing with topics like sentiment and literature analysis. Our publicly available code is designed to be flexible for multiple change detection tasks while minimizing memory usage. Furthermore, we introduce three key challenges for the research community to address in the field of change detection. This includes the difficulty of developing a word sense invariant model, the lack of labeled data for evaluating models in certain domains, and the limited breadth of models in comparison to the vast range of words with evolving meanings. This problem is further compounded by the fact that the majority of words with changing meanings are not part of frequently used datasets. This, in turn, leads to a situation where models optimized on these datasets struggle with out-of-domain data, resulting in an over-reliance on models with word-specific characteristics rather than those with a deeper understanding of language structures. This problem is not unique to change detection but rather a broader issue with models that are trained on datasets with diverse data sets and are subsequently tested on similar datasets with varying parameters. The intricate relationship between knotted protein structures and their functional availability within the cellular environment remains somewhat unclear. Recent research suggests that the presence of knots in proteins is more common than previously thought, with approximately twenty-five percent of naturally occurring proteins exhibiting some level of knotting. It has also been proposed that the space of knotted protein structures is divided into distinct regions, each corresponding to a unique knot type, referred to as a "knot seed". Notwithstanding these advancements, the process by which proteins become knotted and the reason why this phenomenon is so prevalent across nature remain to be fully comprehended. This study introduces the concept of using knotted protein structures in conjunction with advanced mathematical topological tools to predict and visualize the pathways available for bond breaking and reformation. Our research reveals that these predicted pathways differ significantly for proteins with trefoil knots as compared to proteins with their analogues in higher-order knots, specifically with regards to the cross-over number. Moreover, we find that the trefoil knot proteins exhibit a more confined distribution compared to their counterparts in higher-order knots when considering the space of native states. Furthermore, our results indicate that the available space of low-energy states for trefoil knot proteins is separated into two distinct components, each corresponding to a unique set of bending pathways. This distinction enables us to create a classification system for proteins based on their knot types and protein sequences, and to explore the relationship between protein structure and function through the lens of topology. Our research paves the way for a novel approach that integrates experimental and computational studies of knotted proteins, and may yield valuable insights for the broader field of protein folding. This integrated perspective may also offer a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between protein structure, the cellular environment, and protein function, and could provide a useful framework for the development of future proteomics technologies. We have re-examined the constraints on Early Dark Energy (EDE) using a more rigorous statistical approach, taking into account potential discrepancies between EDE and the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) power spectrum. By establishing a simple parameter space that models these discrepancies, we have determined the profile likelihood of EDE given new data from the BOSS and Planck, finding that it falls short of the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimate by a factor of 5 in likelihood units. As a result, the EDE density parameter is constrained to be less than 0.072 at a 95% confidence level, rather than 0.085. This improved constraint, obtained through a more sophisticated statistical method, weakens the constraint by a marginal $2\sigma$ and suggests that future, high-precision surveys will be able to detect even small amounts of EDE. Furthermore, our approach provides a direct comparison of the information content of different datasets, with the implication that the current limit from Planck and BOSS is equivalent to about 80% of the information that will become available from eBOSS and Planck at their current sensitivity levels. With the current precision of the power spectrum, the impact of perturbative gravity on large scales, at $k=0.04$, adds no more than 10% to the overall information about EDE, with the potential for a more significant effect in future analyses. Interestingly, we find that the information about EDE from Planck is primarily derived from a single multipole moment, $\ell=3$, which is sensitive to the starting redshift of the EDE era, while the starting density parameter is instead constrained by a different set of moments in the range $8<\ell<10$. Consequently, the constraints on these two parameters become degenerate, resulting in a first-order phase transition at some starting density parameter for any given EDE starting redshift. This limitation on EDE will continue to apply even with the addition of primordial gravitational waves, with the constraint from Planck and BOSS already approaching the threshold at which the EDE density parameter will be positive in the majority of inflationary models. Moreover, we expect that the starting redshift of the EDE era will be pinned down to within 50-70% of the current value in the next generation of cosmological experiments. We establish that any symplectic mapping class group of a torus in two dimensions is isomorphic to the integer ring of a specific orientation, namely the orientation determined by the symplectic 2-form. This form's differential generates the first Chern class on the blowup of a torus in four dimensions, and we demonstrate that the integer ring of this orientation is self-evident and unchanged under the action of the monodromy associated with the Lefschetz fibration on the blowup's mapping class group. This identification enables us to prove that the monodromy's action on the integer ring of the orientation determines the mapping class group's structure. Furthermore, we find that the (4k-1)-dimensional blowup of a torus in four dimensions possesses a nontrivial action under the stringy Eilenberg-Zilber functor, which is closely related to the Littlewood-Paley functional in harmonic analysis. This fact, in turn, implies that the mapping class group of the (4k-1)-dimensional blowup of a torus is an abelian group that is freely generated by 2^((4k-2)) elements. We also demonstrate that the first Chern class's integer multiples, which are equivalent to the spin^c structures on the blowup of a torus in four dimensions, possess a natural action under the monodromy, and that the intersection form's rank is directly determined by the monodromy's action on the first Chern class's integer multiple parametrizing the mapping class group. This, in conjunction with the fact that the monodromy's action on the first Chern class's integer multiple is injective, allows us to prove that the mapping class group of the complex projective space in four dimensions, which possesses a specific order, is isomorphic to the integer ring of the orientation determined by the symplectic 2-form. The study emphasizes the importance of a unitary and symmetry-breaking pattern in order to yield nontrivial NG bosons. In contrast, bosonic symmetry and unitarity lead to flat potential surfaces, resulting in zero mass NG bosons. The evaluation of the NG boson mass matrix relies on the representation of nonrelativistic NG bosons as bound states of nonrelativistic particle-antiparticle pairs, allowing for the interpretation of the NG theorem within the framework of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics and field theory. A comparison between the contributions of internal and external symmetries in relation to NG bosons is also presented, revealing that only internal symmetries lead to the existence of NG bosons, as exemplified through the Sp(2N) symmetric matrix models of fermion-fermion and boson-boson condensation. A key finding of this research is the proposal of theories involving multiple NG bosons and the prediction of the mass spectra of these theories. A unitary Sp(2N+2) symmetry is applied to a fermionic matrix model, resulting in (N-1) masses of the NG bosons and a single massive state, while a unitary Sp(4N) symmetry yields N distinct mass scales with nonrelativistic power-law behaviors. These theories can be experimentally verified through the measurement of NG boson mass spectra in the regulation of symmetry-breaking phases and the characterization of the low-energy effective theories. A further exploration of the relationship between the Sp(2N) symmetry and the Higgs boson is also discussed. Notably, the formation of La0.7Ca0.3MnO2 nanoclusters on top of the films is more pronounced when they are grown through pinholes, and this occurs because the formation energy of these clusters is lower than that of the continuous films. This understanding has significant implications for the development of electronic devices using Heusler films and it is anticipated that it will pave the way for the creation of novel devices utilizing the unique magnetic properties of these materials. Furthermore, it is proposed that the same principles discovered in this study could be applied to La0.7Ca0.3MnO2 films grown on gold surfaces, which would provide a direct means of observing the cluster formation. This proposal is based on the theory that the opacity of the gold layer would allow it to be observed with light, thus enabling a deeper comprehension of the relationships between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. This knowledge is highly valuable as it gives consideration to the opacity of the substrate when evaluating the modes of epitaxy, a factor that is frequently overlooked in research in this field. This study is significant because it demonstrates that distant and pinhole epitaxy are interconnected and that this understanding has important implications for the development of devices utilizing Heusler films. This is particularly true with regard to the cluster formation, which is influenced by the energy required to form the film and must be considered in research into this phenomenon. This study is also important because it is one of the first examinations of the relationships between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy in La0.7Ca0.3MnO2 films, and it is anticipated that these findings will provide valuable insights for researchers working in this field. This paper establishes a categorical framework that constructs a Hilbert space from these statuses and subsequently determines all possible linear maps between spaces. Conversely, it shows that the physical observables and status are fully defined by this construction. This categorical approach enables the exploration of the underlying principles of the physical process and its associated mathematical structure. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis from cardiac auscultation sounds is challenging for non-specialists.  Our research focuses on developing an automated system to categorize heart sounds into normal and abnormal sounds.  To achieve this, we collected a comprehensive dataset consisting of 2000 heart sounds recorded from 20 different locations on the human body.  Our experimental dataset comprises 9 classes of recording sites with 1112 heart sounds, and each sample is 2.5 seconds long with a frequency of 1000 Hz.  To mimic real-world situations, we added different types of noise to the records.  Our proposed system uses a technique called Mel-GAN, which combines the mel spectrogram transformation of audio signals with a generative adversarial network.  By applying this technique, we achieved a high accuracy rate of 88.5% in categorizing heart sounds.  Compared to existing methods, our approach has the benefit of preserving sensitive medical information contained in heart sounds, as it doesn't require the disclosure of actual heart sound recordings.  We also evaluated the robustness of our system in categorizing heart sounds under various noise conditions and found that it can handle up to 10dB of white noise and 5dB of heart noise before its performance is affected.  Furthermore, we demonstrated that Mel-GAN is capable of recovering distorted heart sounds due to its generative model nature, and the resulting reconstructed sounds achieve a high accuracy rate of 92.6% in classification.  Our research lays the groundwork for the development of a cardiac diagnosis system using cardiac auscultation sounds.  We believe that our approach, though simple, is highly effective and could be applied to other sound classification tasks.  We have made our dataset and source code available for the research community to use.  Our model's performance exceeded our expectations, and we are now working on improving its performance even further.  In addition to classification, we plan to explore other applications of Mel-GAN in cardiac diagnosis, such as heart sound segmentation and diagnosis.  We are also interested in collaborating with medical professionals and other research organizations to advance the development of cardiac diagnosis systems.  We have already initiated discussions with several organizations and are open to hearing from anyone willing to contribute to this project.  We are confident that our approach can be improved through collaboration and would like to invite anyone with expertise in machine learning and cardiac diagnosis to join our research effort. A key finding is that, when the cost discontinuities are one-sided, the strongest solution can be obtained by toggling between the two components of the cost, resulting in an optimal strategy for controlling a system that switches abruptly. Brain tumor segmentation and typing are difficult tasks in medical image analysis, primarily due to variations in tumor morphology and appearance. One factor contributing to these differences is the inclusion of peritumoral eddy defects in Chien Gewei images, which complicate the typing process. Current methods often apply ensemble techniques by aggregating predictions from diverse models, but this does not account for the directional influence of features on tumors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-task network, MAG-Net, which directs feature attention towards tumor areas. By integrating spatial and channel attention mechanisms, MAG-Net is capable of identifying crucial features for tumor detection and typing. To further improve performance, MAG-Net is pre-trained with patch-wise training and applies a multi-task attention mechanism to accommodate feature differences in Chien Gewei images. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate improved segmentation accuracy and a higher classification mean accuracy when compared to state-of-the-art models. Moreover, MAG-Net exhibits invariant performance across different image resolutions. Notably, MAG-Net achieves a mean accuracy of 68.53% in tumor typing on the CHAOS dataset, outperforming existing methods and serving as a basis for further enhancement through the incorporation of typing-specific information. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation environments that can assess a range of key aspects, such as learning rates and transfer abilities. However, existing systems lack a unified framework that can provide comprehensive evaluation in a controlled and standardized way. To address this gap, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation framework that can handle a broad range of tasks, including both simple single-task problems and more complex, hierarchical learning challenges, and is designed to be easily extendable to accommodate custom learning specifications. L2Explorer is an open-source, modular system that is built on top of a robust set of tools and is now available on GitHub. To demonstrate its capabilities, we have developed a range of continuing learning examples that can be run on the evaluation environment, and we have also introduced a new metric called the continuing learning benchmark score, which provides a clear and objective assessment of a model's performance when compared to human experts. This insight spurred a method called PR-Assessment, which filters predictions through a two-stage process. This report outlines the design of an innovative CMOS technology-based system, where data is addressed by multiple concurrent processors that are also memory locations. This system uses a reconfigurable matrix of identical cells, where each cell contains a look-up table and can be programmed to execute a variety of functions. The availability of a suitable framework for reconfiguring these cells in an island-style FPGA architecture remains unclear at present. Furthermore, discovering an appropriate method for reconfiguring the data-addressing concurrent cells within the island architecture is even more complicated. Our solution involves using a special type of cell that can serve as both a data location and a processing unit by incorporating a dual-role input, which allows it to participate in data addressing and receive external input. We demonstrate that this cell can perform complex operations like hashing, modular addition, and binary search, and that multiple such cells can be easily reconfigured to perform many different tasks with minimal reordering of the data, providing a high degree of flexibility. Additionally, we have successfully implemented this system using a combination of analog and digital signals on a Xilinx Virtex-7 FPGA. One example application of this system is a high-performance linear feedback shift register that produces over 100 billion bits of pseudo-random data per second. Another example is a system for generating large amounts of reference data for database queries in seconds, a task that would typically take days by conventional methods. This has significant implications for generating large datasets of pseudorandom numbers, making it an appropriate solution for various problems in scientific research, such as Monte Carlo simulations and molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, we examine the potential for scaling up this system to handle larger datasets and discuss the advantages of using this technology to develop intelligent databases that can analyze their own data. This system has the potential to significantly impact various fields and industries by providing a new means of processing data that is both more efficient and more flexible than conventional methods. In 2019, observations from the Kepler satellite revealed a unusual periodic pattern of brightness from the low-mass star TOI-667 d, occurring every 12.78 days. Researchers proposed linking the star's diminished transit signal to its increased luminosity, suggesting that TOI-667 d has expanded due to heat, possibly resulting from the star's absorption of energy as it spins. We present new data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, supporting the star's irregular rotation period at around 12.76 days and confirming its unusual brightness patterns. Additionally, we find a potential connection between the star's bright spin-down and its companion planet, TOI-667 d, with its effects potentially being influenced by the star's magnetic field's weakness. We consider two possible explanations: first, that the star is ingesting material from its companion, leading to its spin-down; second, that this spin-down could be caused by a transfer of angular momentum from the star to its companion, with both scenarios deserving further investigation. We also suggest that this phenomenon may offer insight into how stars with high angular momentum evolve over time. We examine the concept of robust quantum nonlocality within unextendible product bases (UPBs) and their corresponding correlation networks. UPBs represent a fundamental framework for exploring quantum nonlocality and have far-reaching implications in chemistry and physics for optimizing quantum communication and computation protocols. However, most studies on quantum nonlocality have focused on systems of identical particles, despite the fact that real-world applications often involve systems with diverse particle types. In contrast, we investigate the quantum nonlocality of UPBs in combined systems of spinless fermions and bosons, demonstrating that the associated correlation networks can exhibit robust quantum nonlocality and we develop a metric to quantify this phenomenon. Furthermore, we show that the degree of robust quantum nonlocality can vary significantly, depending on the specific configuration of the system, and that it is closely linked to the structure of the symmetry matrix. Our research provides a clear method for identifying the presence of robust quantum nonlocality and suggests that certain UPBs in combined systems could serve as inherently secure channels for quantum communication. In addition, we find that, in some cases, the degree of robust quantum nonlocality can be maximized by introducing even numbers of bosons, a counter-intuitive outcome given the generally negative connotations associated with unbalanced particle numbers in chemical reactivity theories. Our work also paves the way for further exploration of quantum nonlocality in complex systems and may facilitate the design of robust, quantum nonlocality-based protocols for practical applications. In the realm of quantum chemistry, our discoveries could lead to a reevaluation of chemical reactivity theories and contribute to the development of novel, quantum nonlocality-assisted synthesis pathways for molecules with stabilizing electron pair interactions. In this research, we establish a new inequality, relating nonisotropic $p$-capacity to Minkowski inequality, applicable to functions that map the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$. This inequality broadens existing inequalities of Poincaré and Sobolev type, originally formulated for isometric mappings. Our result also creates a broader context for the recent nonisotropic Sobolev inequality proved by Kuusjer and Hanso, for which we demonstrate a simpler converse. We show that the sharp constant in the conventional Sobolev inequality can be derived from the nonisotropic $p$-capacity, when $p=1$. This connection, in turn, enables us to determine the sharp constant in the nonisotropic Minkowski inequality, when $p=1$, and present an example of a mapping that illustrates how the conventional Minkowski inequality can be greater than its nonisotropic counterpart. We also derive a new inequality, an alternative to the conventional Minkowski inequality, which is relevant to mappings that increase the diameter of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Finally, we prove that any mapping that satisfies the conventional Minkowski inequality when $p=1$ will also satisfy the same inequality for any $p$ in the same range, provided that $p$ is not equal to one. This result holds when the target space has a high enough dimension. This broadens the scope of our main result and provides the groundwork for investigating whether a similar extension is possible when the target space has a dimension less than $n$. This dimension-based limitation likely holds, based on our experience with isometric mappings, for which the sharp constant in the nonisotropic Minkowski inequality increases more slowly in relation to $p$ than the capacity. This suggests that the boundary between inequalities defined by capacity and Minkowski should be at an even more distant value of $p$. However, most of these attacks relied heavily on the knowledge of the model's parameters and architecture, which is not always the case in practical situations. A more realistic approach involves non-inverse attacks, where the adversary does not have access to this information. Currently, the standard method for achieving this involves training the model to classify features that indicate whether it is being attacked or not. This paper proposes a new framework for achieving non-inverse attacks, where the adversary only needs to provide yes/no answers to whether the model misclassified certain images. This information is used to update the model's classification of specific classes without needing access to its internal workings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a real-world image classification scenario. We show that our method is capable of reducing the model's error rate without needing any information about its architecture or parameters. We also find that this approach is relevant to real-world scenarios, where the amount of attack data is limited. This is because it allows the model to learn from just a small number of attack examples. We evaluate our approach through a series of experiments, where we achieve a notable reduction in error rates of up to 20%. This improvement is particularly significant because it indicates that the model is able to learn from just a small number of attack examples. This is a zero-shot knowledge transfer, where the model is able to learn from just a small number of attack examples without needing any additional training. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally challenging, but it becomes manageable when that module has no non-trivial supermodules with simple composition factors other than those of the original module - in other words, when it is multiplicity free. For modules within the family of Weyl modules, over certain Lie algebras and Heisenberg Lie algebras, and for polynomial modules over semisimple algebras, we outline an approach to building their lattice of submodules. Additionally, this method allows us to develop algorithms for determining module composition factors and identifying submodules of given attributes, such as dimension-based or maximal submodules, contributing to a comprehensive understanding of the structure of these modules. Our technique also offers insights into connections between system of inequalities, lattice paths, and module substructures, providing a unifying framework that can be applied across different modules. Exemplary computations with the proposed method are also presented for the F4 Lie algebra and its Weyl modules, demonstrating its practical utility. This research is a follow-up to our prior work on constructing modules with Heisenberg Lie algebras, and we have made our computational data freely available for download. Furthermore, we have established that one of the modules we investigated shares ties with the representation theory of the symmetric group, as explicitly shown in a concurrently published paper by S. Koplak. On the algorithmic front, we have resolved one of the open problems discussed in our prior work, namely finding all submodules of a given module by employing a combination of computational techniques and insights derived from analyzing lattice paths. This solution has implications for solving systems of inequalities with weights, a problem that is itself NP-hard. Nonetheless, we have demonstrated that when the underlying algebra is semisimple, the composition factor decomposition of a module can be determined efficiently, potentially leading to further advancements in this area. This knowledge also has a significant impact on the theory of Lie algebras, as it reveals that the representation theory of these algebras is polynomial for modules within the family of Weyl modules. This means that given a set of simple roots, all submodules of the corresponding Weyl module can be constructed automatically, providing a crucial breakthrough in the field. This development raises another question: what about modules that are not multiplicity free? To address this question, we propose a strategy for dealing with modules that have non-trivial supermodules with simple composition factors other than those of the original module - in other words, when they are not multiplicity free

The Strong Geodetic Problem is a well-known computational problem in mathematics, closely related to graph theory and identification problems. A geodetic set in a graph is the smallest set of points that can identify the others, with the shortest path between any two points being unique. The Strong Geodetic Problem involves determining the smallest number of points in this set. This problem is NP-hard and has been solved optimally for specific graph types, but its computational complexity remains uncertain for most graphs. This paper provides evidence that approximating the solution within a factor better than O(n^2) is impossible, with n representing the total number of points in the graph. Additionally, this paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm for solving the problem efficiently in bipartite graphs. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the computational complexity of the Strong Geodetic Problem. Furthermore, this paper introduces the concept of a "weakly optimal solution," which approximates the optimal solution within a factor of n^2, and proposes a polynomial-time algorithm for determining whether a given solution is weakly optimal. This algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive benchmark tests involving a wide range of random graphs. However, the possibility of improving this approximation factor remains an open question. With respect to the problem of finding an optimal solution, there is a lower bound suggesting that it requires at least n^2 - n approximate solutions before guaranteeing optimality. This lower bound is applicable across any algorithm and provides a benchmark for future research into this problem. Additionally, this paper introduces the concept of a "most recent weakly optimal solution," which could potentially serve as a starting point for further research into approximation algorithms. This paper's results and the associated challenges it poses may also contribute to a better understanding of other computational problems, such as the minimum connected dominating set problem and the strong connected dominating set problem. With respect to graph theory, this paper's results may provide valuable insights, given that many graph theory problems have underlying structures similar to those of computational complexity theory. Therefore, problems such as determining the smallest dominating set or the smallest independent dominating set, which have fundamental connections to mathematics and computer science, are of significant interest. As such, identifying whether approximating the solution to these problems is possible could lead to a better understanding of these fundamental problems. This paper's results provide a contribution towards resolving this issue and could serve as a benchmark for further research into these problems. A fundamental challenge in mimicry learning is addressed, where a student model, leveraging a limited dataset, effectively mimics a confident teacher model based on a vast amount of data. This study focuses on mimicry tasks where the target function differs significantly from the available training data, as is the case with various real-world adaptations, noisy labeled data, and data with varying importance. Unlike existing mimicry algorithms, which require high-quality supervised data, this study explores the potential for a student to learn from imperfect supervised data, such as unlabelled data with noise, or data with different weights. A theoretical analysis confirms that a student can achieve near-optimal performance, even with noisy labeled data, and this result is further validated through experiments on artificial and real-world datasets, demonstrating the advantages of this approach over traditional mimicry methods. Additionally, this study finds that its simple variant, where the target function is unknown, reduces to an unsupervised learning problem, worth exploring in its own right. It introduces an appropriate metric to evaluate the degree of mimicry and a practical approach to implement it. TRAIL, an algorithm based on this metric, is first considered a generalization of the 1970s ridge regression algorithm and offers a theoretical performance guarantee. It is applicable to various settings, including those with noisy labeled data, and its advantages over existing mimicry methods are clear. TRAIL is a publicly available Python package. It can be co-trained with the teacher and used as a pretraining method for the student alone. TRAIL's performance is compared to that of multiple strong baseline algorithms, and it consistently achieves better results on diverse imitation tasks, as evaluated using multiple metrics. TRAIL is a highly adaptable algorithm that is both efficient and simple, with a short training time and compact model size. It is suitable for a wide range of imitation tasks, including those with complex data, as demonstrated through its performance on real-world datasets. It is noted that while TRAIL offers optimal performance in mimicry learning, its exact application as a solution to complex problems may require additional tuning and optimization. Moreover, further research is needed to explore its potential benefits and potential limitations in solving complex, real-world problems. It is proposed that future work should focus on: providing a formal definition for mimicry learning in the presence of target uncertainty, developing new algorithms tailored to specific data conditions, and exploring new evaluation metrics to measure the performance of mimicry learning algorithms. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding process can be completed in approximately 0.45% of the original computations, achieving a 99.55% error-correction success rate on the BWBW distribution, which is only 2% lower than the optimal performance. We demonstrate that nearly all 0.45% percentage reduction in computations results in a 2% percentage increase in error-correction success rate, based on an in-depth computational analysis. By contrast, the recently introduced minimum-free-state decoding criterion has a 99.06% error-correction success rate on the BWBW distribution, which is 0.49% lower than the optimal performance and 0.06% lower than the simple uniform metric criterion. Moreover, our proposed metric can be applied to the design of maximum-error-path codes with superior error-correction performance, achieving a 99.81% error-correction success rate on the BWBW distribution with an average free state of 0.84. Additionally, we investigate and characterize the critical factors that influence the performance of various decoding criteria and metric functions. We show that the primary factor affecting the 99.49% error-correction success rate of the simple uniform metric function is the large number of small-size children with zero polarization, which accounts for 76.8% of all children. Consequently, we propose a new definition for the polarization of a node in the trellis structure, which can be used to further reduce the number of small-size children with zero polarization to below 10%, thereby achieving a 99.81% error-correction success rate with an average free state of 0.84. Thompson's group V using its action on the interval I, and prove that the V word problem is equivalent to solving a related problem concerning the interval I, which we term the "interval problem". This interval problem can be expressed as a first-order logic statement about the order structure of V's action on I. Notably, the interval problem for V is undecidable, which provides a new proof of the undecidability of the V word problem. This result demonstrates that the word problems of groups with order structures similar to V's may also be undecidable. A quantum system under constant periodic influence develops a steady state that is key to implementing robust quantum processes, and understanding its dynamics is crucial. To describe this steadily to vary state with time, we use a rotating frame of reference and identify the essential and quasi-essential Floquet operators that dictate the behavior through their application to the system's state over one period. This description is highly informative and enables calculation of the steady state's properties, even for complex systems, providing a pivotal tool for quantum technology applications. In the case of a driven qubit system, its dynamics can be described using the T1 relaxation time and precise temporal control to manipulate the steady state's properties. We demonstrate that a condition previously considered necessary, where the driving and relaxation rates are much slower than the transition frequency, is not necessary to apply this description, making it possible to model systems where this condition is not met, such as certain atomic systems. This knowledge is further utilized to develop a quantum heat current indicator that is independent of temperature and reveals that, in the regime where the driving and relaxation rates are much slower than the transition frequency, the heat current shows an asymmetric distribution on the two sides of the qubit, evolving over time to follow the signature of a frequency up to four times its natural frequency. This behavior is expected to be observable with current technology and may provide a means of controlling quantum heat transfer. Additionally, this control could enable a quantum heat engine to achieve a higher efficiency than the Carnot limit by carefully balancing the drive and relaxation processes. Furthermore, this study indicates that, in order to implement a not-in-equilibrium steady state effectively, it is not sufficient to control the drive and relaxation processes, as even when these processes are closely matched, the system's behavior will still vary significantly with time. This conclusion is reached through an analysis of the system's dynamics when its transition frequency is much higher than the driving and relaxation rates, a condition that is often met in experimental implementations of quantum systems. A set of integers is considered p/q-identifiable if its members' simplest fractions have a common denominator that is identifiable as q. Recently, J. V. Armitage established that all sets with a density greater than 1/2 are 2q-identifiable, and we extend this by showing that no 1/q-identifiable set exists with a given density. We also demonstrate that many large 2q-identifiable sets contain a nonempty 1q-identifiable subset. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate structure of this scheme with approximately 4 million active participants and over 4 million USD in daily transactions. By investing a minimum of 0.25 USD and up to 1 million USD, users can contribute to Forsage through three distinct investment levels, with returns generated from a complex network of interconnected smart contracts designed to mask payment histories. By examining Forsage's transaction data, our findings reveal a robust, multi-level pyramid structure, with participants recruited through a continuous stream of lower-ranking referree payments, exceeding $1 billion in total. Our empirical research on Forsage also raises important questions about the role of cryptocurrency exchanges in enabling such schemes and the need for more stringent guidelines to govern the inclusion of suspicious activity-based addresses in blockchain-based platforms. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been developed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct steps, first transforming the complex problem into a simpler form and then finding the ground state of the transformed Hamiltonian, which is assumed to be non-interacting and represent different spin variables. One key issue is synchronizing their ambulatory state, which is influenced by various factors such as muscle function, prosthetic technology, and mental state. The underlying theory is comprised of a family of ordered pairs, each representing a co-ary n-ary operation and its corresponding arity. Isomorphisms between these structures are closely related to ordered pairs of functions, which induce a notion of symmetry. The algorithmic isomorphism test can be viewed through the lens of these functions and symmetry relations. Building on existing work, we establish that a key component, the triadic structure, contains the essential information for isomorphisms. Moreover, we define a new notion of isomorphism, termed 'trim isomorphism', which relies exclusively on this core component. This streamlined concept enables us to prove the efficacy of the algorithmic isomorphism test. Additionally, we explore the scope of this test in the broader context of distributive structures. Finally, we discuss potential connections between this research and existing results on first-order formulas. Large-scale quantum computing relies on coding that allows for error correction, with the coding process being highly complex and prone to faults. In this research, we focus on developing a new coding system that can adapt to changing conditions and automatically learn from experience to minimize residual errors. This codification process can be viewed as a problem of sequential decision-making when the consequences of actions are uncertain and vary depending on the state of the system. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, this method isn't practical because it lacks a relationship between measurements and the variable of interest. A more practical approach is leap metrology, which involves multiple quantum states with varying exposures to a unknown variable before making a single measurement to obtain the most useful information. This process is applied to a dual-cavity setup, where two cavities are both exposed to the same light field, but one contains a variable phase shift. A new method is found to determine the phase shift with greater precision than would be achievable otherwise. We investigated how interactions between two agents can solve for the contextual linear gimbal parameters without sharing the context, using a simple scheme that involves each agent alternately observing the other's action and receiving a related reward. This work further investigates the extreme performance benefits of optimized versus binary power control in K-user interference networks, building on previous research. Initially, it was observed that the general DoF gain from optimal power control, as opposed to binary switching, increases sublinearly with the number of users K. However, this study aims to uncover the exact relationship of this gain with respect to K. To achieve this, a more refined analysis is applied, utilizing an earlier proposed graph theory framework. Specifically, the concept of a user being "well-served" is redefined to better fit binary power settings, resulting in a more complex set of relationships among users. Consequently, the analysis of optimal power control performances becomes significantly more intricate, giving rise to user pairs with "flappy" and "towering" relationships. Ultimately, the limits of binary power control can be surpassed at a rate roughly proportional to the square root of K, as the benefits of optimized power control across these new metrics continue to suggest a broad applicability. Additionally, the scope of modern wireless communication systems is explored, encompassing applications beyond just interference networks. The measures of performance gain under optimal power control, as compared to binary power control, are found to be at least equal to approximately 2.45*sqrt(K), and no more than 3.01*sqrt(K). The methods employed in this study can also be applied to evaluate the extremal gain of binary power control over a converged scenario, resulting in a lower bound of at least 1.45*sqrt(K). The theoretical limits of both optimal and binary power control are then compared, with the former showing signs of convergence with the latter at around 10 to 12 user pairs in an 8-user 3-user pair network, highlighting the enduring superiority of optimal power control. The recently proposed binary power triplets, derived from optimal power quadruplets, are found to provide a gain of approximately 2.25*sqrt(K), indicating that the increased complexity of optimal power control can yield a significant further benefit of at least 0.75*sqrt(K) over this new baseline in an 8-user 3-user pair network, concluding the study. The outcomes of this research are subject to the precision of the analytical methods employed and provide valuable insights into the extreme performance benefits of optimized power control, out of sequence power control, and binary power triads in large interference networks, with the former exceeding the latter by at least 1.45*sqrt(K). This study proposes a new integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in DEM that maintains accuracy. Due to the slow nature of grain collisions, hundreds of time steps may be spent on a single collision, necessitating a more efficient approach than traditional resolution. Our method leverages the inherent symmetry of normal grain collisions to significantly reduce the size of the time step used in DEM simulations, allowing for larger time steps while maintaining accuracy. A demonstration simulation of an inclined chute flow shows our method's new time step size has a negligible effect on collision detection, whereas the method fails without a minimum time step size. Nevertheless, our results indicate that this method does not accurately capture the behavior in regions with high shear rates. Furthermore, a simulation of a fluidized bed reveals that this method can result in negative normal velocity components during collisions, an artifact caused by the method's focus on resolving collisions rather than following the equations of motion. As a result, over 30% of collisions in the fluidized bed simulation became'stuck' with zero progress in over 100 time steps, an issue addressed by introducing a collision resolution failure criterion to prevent such cases in future DEM simulations. Despite these challenges, both simulations show that DEM simulations can be improved by reducing frictional forces in areas with high shear rates. Our proposed method achieves a notable 3 times performance improvement in the inclined chute simulation and 5 times in the fluidized bed simulation. To further validate our method, a comparison with particle tracking velocimetry measurements in a range of flow rates is planned for the future. Our method's failure to accurately capture behavior in regions with high shear rates suggests that an alternative approach is required to resolve collisions in such flows. Due to the fundamental differences between DEM simulations and actual grain collisions, our method is not a universally applicable solution, largely because two dimensions are insufficient in modeling the behavior in flows with high shear rates. Consequently, a new DEM framework with an adaptive time step for resolving collisions in different flow regimes is required. This framework should integrate our method in low shear rate regions and alternative methods in regions with high shear rates. Systematic measurements of collision duration are also necessary to better understand the impacts of flow regimes on collision duration. Additionally, the effects of normal and tangential velocity ratios on collision duration should be investigated to create a collision duration profile, guiding the development of an optimal DEM simulation protocol. A major challenge for legged robots is balancing stability and forward momentum when moving on deformable ground. This project involves creating a simplified one-legged hopping robot model that interacts with a soft, bouncing surface powered by a continuous ground reaction force. Unlike previous robotic studies, this model includes a critical phase where the robot's foot and surrounding ground blend into a complex shape affecting its motion. To overcome these difficulties, researchers developed an innovative method combining bond graph modeling and numerical simulation. By identifying and controlling key dynamics, they successfully modified the robot's design to manage challenging ground conditions. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach, enabling the robot to maintain stability and momentum on uneven terrain. This knowledge can also be applied to multi-legged robots, like humans, benefiting from a similar phase plane feedback control strategy. A video showcasing the robot's performance on various ground shapes is available at https://youtu.be/9J3H2HLo9QI. Through this work, the application of modern modeling techniques and simulations provides a path for developing more advanced robotics solutions to tackle complex interactions with dynamic environments. A previously unrecognized phenomenon, a droplet electrohydrodynamic fan, is exhibited when a liquid droplet, situated within an electric field-generated force pattern, meets specific conditions including the presence of an adjacent solid surface and particular air flow velocities. Understanding negation in written text is a crucial skill that supports effective reading comprehension. Despite being a fundamental concept in language and widely employed in various contexts, negation's implications are often misunderstood. The authors propose the CONDAQA dataset, containing 5,000 Human-annotated questions that require reasoning about negation in a diverse set of articles from Wikipedia, as a resource to advance the development of models that can comprehend negation. This dataset's unique feature lies in its emphasis on the relationship between statements in the text's implicit or explicit negative form. The authors demonstrate current leading models' limited capacity to understand negation by achieving only 50% accuracy on this dataset despite performing well on other reading comprehension tasks. This insight prompts the authors to explore models that are specifically designed to understand the implications of negation and the results show considerable improvement, up to 76%, indicating that negation's comprehension is a key challenge for current reading comprehension models. Furthermore, the authors observe that pre-trained models' performance on questions that focus on explicit negation performs better than those that focus on implicit negation, leading to an opportunity for future research to explore the comprehension of implicit negation through modeling the underlying semantics of language. The authors apply a contrastive learning approach that involves expanding the CONDAQA dataset with negation-aware descriptions, which leads to a further increase in performance, up to 79%, indicating that combinatorial semantics that is inspired by Montague's System does not capture the comprehension of negation. Additionally, the authors discover that the application of this approach results in models that are more adept at handling complex negation queries and encompassing the implicit negative statements presented in the Wikipedia articles, resulting in a score of 61% on the explicit questions and 44% on the implicit questions. The authors acknowledge that the datasets precluding the comprehension of abstract concepts and the models' limited generalization capabilities to other texts constitute significant limitations. Moreover, the CompreHending Negation and Case-Logic (CHNCL) model introduced by the authors, which incorporates a Case-Logic Module that models the implications of negation and delivers outstanding performance, indicates that the comprehension of negation is largely achieved through the use of case information. The authors propose that the CONDAQA dataset offers a compelling case for the development of models that are capable of comprehending the implications of negation and the results obtained with the CHNCL model provide a compelling evidence that the comprehension of negation is a key challenge for the current leading models. Large-scale information networks, typically encountered in online social networks and the web, contain vast numbers of elements that pose challenges for current computational methods. Due to memory constraints, widely used approaches are often limited to analyzing mini-batch representations of the network, thereby hindering applications that require global network properties. Existing solutions that aim to overcome this limitation often focus on specific structures, such as communities or central nodes, neglecting others like spans and fronts. To address this gap, we propose an open-source C++ framework called NetCombiner, capable of computing various network structures preserving their original definition. To demonstrate its utility, we apply NetCombiner to three use cases: one related to computer vision and two related to natural language processing. By leveraging this framework, researchers can explore new ways to model network structures while also exploring its potential for solving other real-world problems. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development: quantum annealing is gradual and deliberate, whereas quenching is abrupt and spontaneous. This distinction highlights the significance of understanding how systems evolve following a quick change, particularly when this change is part of a quantum annealing process. We investigate the consequences of suddenly introducing and increasing an "annealing interval" in a quantum system that is analogous to the Ising model and features a exact cover constraint, with the goal of determining whether this leads to the formation of a steady-state solution that corresponds to a minimum of the Hamiltonian. Instead, we find that the system responds to the quench in an uncontrolled manner, resulting in the emergence of multiple peak states, along with a distinct temporal behavior that is influenced by both the specific quench rate and system spacing. Notably, we observe that certain systems exhibit peak states with distinct characteristics that are related to system geometry and are embedded within a sea of unrelated states. Furthermore, we find that the probability of observing these peak states increases as the quench rate is reduced, or as the system is expanded in certain directions. Using a dual-band model, we examine the infinite-layer nickelate $(NCNO)_\infty$ and find that it exhibits both correlation and doping effects.  Nickel valence can be understood through a screening mechanism, where it is reduced by doping or correlation, or by shifting one or more of the hybridized $3d$-$4p$ bands in the correct range for $d$-wave pairing.  However, this increase in nickel valence comes at the cost of reducing the pairing strength.  We believe that this screening effect can be lessened in experiments by increasing the on-site repulsion at the cost of attracting pairs, a move that restores higher nickel valence while maintaining $d$-wave pairing.  What results is a model that may offer insight into the unusual normal state of $(NCNO)_\infty$, potentially explaining anomalous magnetic response and a normal-to-superconducting phase transition when the lattice is constrained, all while this superconducting state is achieved through pairing with attractive interactions rather than the emission of magnetic excitations.  This solution offers an alternative to previously proposed solutions involving competition between different orders, and suggests that constraint of lattice expansion may enhance the superconducting state.  Finally, we propose that $(NCNO)_\infty$ with $x=0.125$ is the most suitable material to test our model using spectroscopic measurements of screening and pairing, with the potential to significantly influence both theory and experimentation in solid-state physics.  What is presented here is an extension of an idea initially described in Ref.~[\citestyle{cites_key}Kato_2020_jpsj].  What is new in this version of the paper is the demonstration that correlation can also induce screening in the dual-band model, a discovery that is then used to resolve the valence of the nickel in the infinite-layer nickelate, a question that has been a subject of debate amongst scientists.  What is the base for this resolution is the consideration of three different situations:  the case where neither of the hybridized $3d$-$4p$ bands is in the correlation range,  the case where one of the bands is in the correlation range,  and the case where both of the hybridized $3d$-$4p$ bands are in the correlation range.
